extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," accusing the three news organizations of reporting "fake news" about him and his administration. "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social . "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." Asked about the ban during an Oval Office appearance later Friday, Trump said , "You need a free press. You need a fair press and an honest press. They purposely write negative news." The White House referred TheWrap to those remarks but did not clarify how the ban would be implemented or whether it would revoke reporters' credentials, restrict their access to the White House grounds or exclude the outlets from briefings, presidential events and the press pool. A CNN spokesperson told TheWrap: "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right." A Politico spokesperson said, "Politico will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them. The claims that Politico received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked." In his post, Trump falsely claimed that MSNBC changed its name to MS NOW "due to lack of viewership and credibility." The cable network rebranded in November 2025 because it was separating from NBCUniversal as part of Comcast's spinoff of Versant and could no longer use NBC's name and peacock logo. Versant said in a regulatory filing that the rebranding was announced "in connection with the Separation." Trump also described Politico as the recipient of an "illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription" from the federal government under former President Joe Biden. The figure referred to subscriptions purchased across government agencies, primarily for Politico Pro, the company's specialized policy-information service—not a single payment intended to keep the news organization operating. Both the Biden and Trump administrations paid for news-service subscriptions, according to a FactCheck.org review . The announcement marks Trump's latest escalation against news organizations whose coverage he opposes. The AP sued, arguing that it was being punished for its editorial choices. A federal judge initially ordered the administration to restore the outlet's access , although an appeals court later allowed the restrictions to remain in place while the litigation continued. CNN's inclusion could also affect the traditional television pool, through which networks rotate responsibility for providing video coverage of the president to other news organizations. extraction.body: Watch: Trump says ban on some news outlets from White House is "because they're fake news" Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets. An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported. Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized. Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him." Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked. CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated. Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass. All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars". MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy". Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. And CNN said, "we have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right". In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years". Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news." Analysis: Trump escalates media fight after week of setbacks Trump says he is banning CNN and Politico from White House Judge strikes down 'superfluous' Trump lawsuit against the New York Times The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) - the independent, non-profit group that represents journalists who cover the US presidency - called on the administration "to immediately restore" access to the journalists and accused it of violating the First Amendment. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News. Heinrich said that the Americans, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected in their coverage "regardless of whether government officials view it favorably". "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting." Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called Trump's White House ban illegal and unconstitutional. A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional". "The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media. It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC. Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing. Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

extraction.body: UPDATED, with hearing date: CNN , Politico and MS NOW sued Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex. In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit stated. Related Stories News BBC Holding Final Interviews For Next News Chief, With Four Contenders Still In Frame News Ben Affleck Doesn't "Worry About SkyNet" When It Comes To AI; "It's Another Form Of Computing" The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Watch on Deadline The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool assignment for Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York. The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. CNN, Politico and MS NOW are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. The news outlets’ lawsuit was assigned to the same judge, Timothy J. Kelly, who presided over Acosta’s case. He set a hearing via videoconference for Wednesday, and set Tuesday as a deadline for the Trump response. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Boutrous said in a statement that the ban was a “direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process.” He added, “This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, Kelly ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets’ correspondents. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic. Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy. Comments On Deadline Hollywood are monitored. So don't go off topic, don't impersonate anyone, and don't get your facts wrong. They don’t have the money. CNN will back down under Ellison and MS NOW does not have the cash as Versant. Politico too. How much do you think it costs to file a court case? Because at least as far as Versant is concerned, that’s the only cost to use since they have their own in-house legal department. The gaslighting! Your side are supposedly Constitutionalists yet the 1st Amendment (Free Speech and Freedom of the Press incase you weren’t aware) can be selectively applied? Not sure where you were all educated, but that’s not how it works. Spend 1 week reading AP and Reuters only instead of Fox News, social media, and Truth Social, and you’ll see what’s actually happening in the world. They write facts with no agenda. Things will look different, I promise. Earlier this year when the authoritarian-in-chief tried to do the same thing with the Associated Press, he lost in court. Absolutely, they will continue. This is a fight over the First Amendment of the Constitution of the United States which protects the press, and the world is watching. passages: UPDATED, with hearing date: CNN , Politico and MS NOW sued Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex.

In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit stated. Related Stories News BBC Holding Final Interviews For Next News Chief, With Four Contenders Still In Frame News Ben Affleck Doesn't "Worry About SkyNet" When It Comes To AI; "It's Another Form Of Computing"

The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Watch on Deadline

The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool assignment for Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York.

The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions.

“President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.”

The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster.

The news outlets’ lawsuit was assigned to the same judge, Timothy J. Kelly, who presided over Acosta’s case. He set a hearing via videoconference for Wednesday, and set Tuesday as a deadline for the Trump response.

In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.”
The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants.

Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
Boutrous said in a statement that the ban was a “direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process.”

He added, “This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.”

In 2018, in the case of Acosta, Kelly ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.”

The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets’ correspondents. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban.
“Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked.
Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations.

In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings.

Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic.

extraction.body: Source: Chip Somodevilla / Getty Welcome back for another edition of Surviving Trump, our round-up of the latest in President Donald Trump’s lies, corruption, and all-around Trump-foolery. Apparently, this is a series that would undoubtedly get NewsOne banned from the White House press corps, not because we’re lying about the lying-est president in recent history, but because Trump’s orangey-white supremacist butt gets hurt when the overwhelming majority of news outlets fail to report anything positive about him, which is pretty much always, and for the same reason virtually no media outlets would report anything positive about fire, brimstone, and flying locusts filling the skies. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about. Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication. Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot. 6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world. Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets. He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip. On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional. Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House. Trump is even out here touting Breitbart News — yes, that Breitbart News — as its beacon of truth and “the only outlet that covers him fairly.” Come on, y’all — this is a man who loves “fake news,” is “fake news,” and relies on “fake news” as his only political refuge. He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him. Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News. Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr. It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial. Speaking of AI, Trump’s love affair with AI slop continues to be an every-hour-on-the-hour thing, as do his self-revealed fantasies of global authoritarianism. In the image, the only nation clearly shown is Greenland, which likely means this post was inspired by the new Greenland deal he’s been boasting about, even though it’s the same deal we have had with the nation for 75 years, with a few more bells and whistles. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump claimed in a lengthy social media post. The U.S. has had a deal allowing it a largely unfettered military presence in Greenland since 1951, but the new deal is reportedly different because it makes U.S. military presence in the region permanent, according to Trump, and bars non-NATO nations from establishing their own presence in Greenland. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. He also didn’t seem to understand that calling his current term “THREE” undermined the message he was going for. On Friday, Trump posted what he called his “TOP 25 TRUMP ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF TERM THREE,” which included the termination of “scams” that only he has declared a scam, like the green energy efforts he has long declared war on, the “8 wars” he keeps claiming he ended without giving explicit examples, his National Guard deployments, which have largely been blocked by federal judges, including SCOTUS, because they’re unconstitutional, and the aforementioned drop in crime that he is in no way responsible for. Of course, Trump lying about his non-accomplishments is just par for the MAGA course, but his insistence that he’s actually served three terms because he still can’t handle his loss in 2020 should be a concern to anyone who wants to believe the nation isn’t being run by a poster child for mental health awareness for senior citizens. extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," accusing the three news organizations of reporting "fake news" about him and his administration. "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social . "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." Asked about the ban during an Oval Office appearance later Friday, Trump said , "You need a free press. You need a fair press and an honest press. They purposely write negative news." The White House referred TheWrap to those remarks but did not clarify how the ban would be implemented or whether it would revoke reporters' credentials, restrict their access to the White House grounds or exclude the outlets from briefings, presidential events and the press pool. A CNN spokesperson told TheWrap: "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right." A Politico spokesperson said, "Politico will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them. The claims that Politico received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked." In his post, Trump falsely claimed that MSNBC changed its name to MS NOW "due to lack of viewership and credibility." The cable network rebranded in November 2025 because it was separating from NBCUniversal as part of Comcast's spinoff of Versant and could no longer use NBC's name and peacock logo. Versant said in a regulatory filing that the rebranding was announced "in connection with the Separation." Trump also described Politico as the recipient of an "illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription" from the federal government under former President Joe Biden. The figure referred to subscriptions purchased across government agencies, primarily for Politico Pro, the company's specialized policy-information service—not a single payment intended to keep the news organization operating. Both the Biden and Trump administrations paid for news-service subscriptions, according to a FactCheck.org review . The announcement marks Trump's latest escalation against news organizations whose coverage he opposes. extraction.body: Watch: Trump says ban on some news outlets from White House is "because they're fake news" Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets. An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported. Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized. Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him." Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked. CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated. Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass. All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars". MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy". Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. And CNN said, "we have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right". In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years". Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news." Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
"The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass.

An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".

In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit stated. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Watch on Deadline The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool assignment for Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York. The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. CNN, Politico and MS NOW are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. The news outlets’ lawsuit was assigned to the same judge, Timothy J. Kelly, who presided over Acosta’s case. He set a hearing via videoconference for Wednesday, and set Tuesday as a deadline for the Trump response. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Boutrous said in a statement that the ban was a “direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process.” He added, “This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, Kelly ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets’ correspondents. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. extraction.body: Source: Chip Somodevilla / Getty Welcome back for another edition of Surviving Trump, our round-up of the latest in President Donald Trump’s lies, corruption, and all-around Trump-foolery. Apparently, this is a series that would undoubtedly get NewsOne banned from the White House press corps, not because we’re lying about the lying-est president in recent history, but because Trump’s orangey-white supremacist butt gets hurt when the overwhelming majority of news outlets fail to report anything positive about him, which is pretty much always, and for the same reason virtually no media outlets would report anything positive about fire, brimstone, and flying locusts filling the skies. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about. Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication. Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot. 6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world. Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets. He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip. On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional. Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House. Trump is even out here touting Breitbart News — yes, that Breitbart News — as its beacon of truth and “the only outlet that covers him fairly.” Come on, y’all — this is a man who loves “fake news,” is “fake news,” and relies on “fake news” as his only political refuge. He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him. Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News. Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr. It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial. Speaking of AI, Trump’s love affair with AI slop continues to be an every-hour-on-the-hour thing, as do his self-revealed fantasies of global authoritarianism. In the image, the only nation clearly shown is Greenland, which likely means this post was inspired by the new Greenland deal he’s been boasting about, even though it’s the same deal we have had with the nation for 75 years, with a few more bells and whistles. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump claimed in a lengthy social media post. The U.S. has had a deal allowing it a largely unfettered military presence in Greenland since 1951, but the new deal is reportedly different because it makes U.S. military presence in the region permanent, according to Trump, and bars non-NATO nations from establishing their own presence in Greenland. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. He also didn’t seem to understand that calling his current term “THREE” undermined the message he was going for. On Friday, Trump posted what he called his “TOP 25 TRUMP ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF TERM THREE,” which included the termination of “scams” that only he has declared a scam, like the green energy efforts he has long declared war on, the “8 wars” he keeps claiming he ended without giving explicit examples, his National Guard deployments, which have largely been blocked by federal judges, including SCOTUS, because they’re unconstitutional, and the aforementioned drop in crime that he is in no way responsible for. Of course, Trump lying about his non-accomplishments is just par for the MAGA course, but his insistence that he’s actually served three terms because he still can’t handle his loss in 2020 should be a concern to anyone who wants to believe the nation isn’t being run by a poster child for mental health awareness for senior citizens. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about.
Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication.
Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot.
6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world.
Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets.

He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.

It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip.

On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional.
Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House.

He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him.
Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News.

Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr.
It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial.

sources.title: Judge dismisses Chegg and Penske antitrust lawsuits targeting Google AI search
passages: In a setback for publishers worried about the effects of AI search, a US federal judge has dismissed lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google.
The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites.
However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.
The lawsuits were filed in 2025 , and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year.
Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content.
This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic.
Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic .
Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out.
Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply.
And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search.
He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law .
However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case.
The court acknowledges AI search comes with consequences, but it’s not an antitrust issue.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta.
Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm.

Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content. This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic. Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic . Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out. These arguments did not sway the judge, who noted that Google’s implicit agreement with websites is not legally relevant. “Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.” Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply. And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search. He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law . However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case. While Google is getting the dismissal it wanted, it doesn’t come away looking particularly good. Mehta recognizes that Google’s approach to AI search may be unfair to web publishers even if it’s not illegal. “The court does not treat Plaintiffs’ alleged harms lightly,” he wrote. “Nor is it unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in, and the knock-on consequences to journalists, educators, and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation.” This case essentially comes down to the nature of innovation. Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm. However, not all economic harm that may befall a company is the product of an illegal act. Mehta says that antitrust laws cannot be applied in place of legislative action just because something feels unfair: “The court is bound to apply the law only as it is written, not how the court or any party believes it ought to be.” Google will undoubtedly face more legal challenges over AI search, but it’s going to be an uphill battle in US courts absent new legislation, and lawmakers have been slow to adapt to the AI era. Publishers may have more luck overseas. The European Commission is currently considering these same questions, and it tends to take a dimmer view of Big Tech’s conduct. The UK has also ordered Google to provide an AI opt-out for sites that want to remain in organic search results. Google is exploring ways to pay sites directly for contributing to AI answers, but its pilot program is reportedly not going over well with publishers. In a setback for publishers worried about the effects of AI search, a US federal judge has dismissed lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google. The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites. However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.

The lawsuits were filed in 2025 , and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year. Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content. This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic. Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic . Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out.

These arguments did not sway the judge, who noted that Google’s implicit agreement with websites is not legally relevant. “Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.”

Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply. And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search. He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law . However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case.

While Google is getting the dismissal it wanted, it doesn’t come away looking particularly good. Mehta recognizes that Google’s approach to AI search may be unfair to web publishers even if it’s not illegal.

“The court does not treat Plaintiffs’ alleged harms lightly,” he wrote. “Nor is it unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in, and the knock-on consequences to journalists, educators, and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation.”

This case essentially comes down to the nature of innovation. Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm. However, not all economic harm that may befall a company is the product of an illegal act. Mehta says that antitrust laws cannot be applied in place of legislative action just because something feels unfair: “The court is bound to apply the law only as it is written, not how the court or any party believes it ought to be.”

Google will undoubtedly face more legal challenges over AI search, but it’s going to be an uphill battle in US courts absent new legislation, and lawmakers have been slow to adapt to the AI era. Publishers may have more luck overseas. The European Commission is currently considering these same questions, and it tends to take a dimmer view of Big Tech’s conduct. The UK has also ordered Google to provide an AI opt-out for sites that want to remain in organic search results.
Google is exploring ways to pay sites directly for contributing to AI answers, but its pilot program is reportedly not going over well with publishers.

relevantPassages.text: According to a report by news agency Reuters, an order issued by US District Judge Amit Mehta of the District of Columbia dismissed both complaints, concluding that the publishers’ claims that Google violated federal antitrust statutes “fail to get out of the starting gate.”What Chegg and Penske claimed in their lawsuitsChegg and Penske Media, the parent company behind publications such as Rolling Stone, Variety and Billboard, brought the lawsuits last year, claiming Google engaged in anticompetitive conduct by tying search visibility to AI summaries.

In a truly competitive search market, Google would be compelled to license their material or pay to train its AI systems.Google denied any wrongdoing, countering that it is under no legal mandate to index external web pages under publishers' self-selected terms.What the ruling saidJudge Mehta rejected the claims that the search engine owed publishers guaranteed web traffic in return for crawling publicly accessible pages.“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free,” Mehta wrote.

The plaintiffs argued that Google effectively forced publishers to permit their digital content to be summarised by AI Overviews if they wished to stay indexed in Google Search.They also claimed Google scraped and synthesised their web pages directly on results pages sharply reduced referral traffic, eroding their advertising and subscription revenue.

It is simply how a general search engine works.”While Mehta noted he was not “unsympathetic to the situation of publishers and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation,” he held that antitrust statutes cannot serve as a stand-in for congressional action to remedy the economic fallout of technological innovation.You use AI every day.

coreStoryFacts.text: A federal judge has dismissed a pair of antitrust lawsuits filed by Chegg and Rolling Stone parent company Penske Media Corporation, which accused Google of driving away web traffic with its AI-powered search features, as reported earlier by Reuters.
This week, The Information reported that Google is paying around 100 publishers for their contributions to AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini as part of a pilot program.

It is simply how a general search engine works.” Mehta adds that the court is not “unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in,” but writes that antitrust rules can’t replace a legislative body’s decision to address the economic impact of “new innovation.” Meanwhile, publishers continue to see effects of Google’s AI-powered search overhaul, with traffic to news outlets and small websites taking a steep dive.
US District Judge Amit Mehta takes Google’s side in a ruling on Wednesday, writing that PMC and Chegg’s claims don’t stand up to antitrust law.
Judge Mehta, who made a landmark antitrust ruling against Google in 2024, disagrees with Chegg and PMC’s claims.
The publishers alleged Google’s practices diverted traffic away from their sites, hurting their revenue.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” Mehta writes.
In a setback for publishers worried about the effects of AI search, a US federal judge has dismissed lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google.
The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites.
However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.
The lawsuits were filed in 2025 , and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year.
Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content.
This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic.
Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic .
Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out.
Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply.
And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search.
He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law .
However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case.
The court acknowledges AI search comes with consequences, but it’s not an antitrust issue.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta.
Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm.

passages: According to a report by news agency Reuters, an order issued by US District Judge Amit Mehta of the District of Columbia dismissed both complaints, concluding that the publishers’ claims that Google violated federal antitrust statutes “fail to get out of the starting gate.”What Chegg and Penske claimed in their lawsuitsChegg and Penske Media, the parent company behind publications such as Rolling Stone, Variety and Billboard, brought the lawsuits last year, claiming Google engaged in anticompetitive conduct by tying search visibility to AI summaries.

In a truly competitive search market, Google would be compelled to license their material or pay to train its AI systems.Google denied any wrongdoing, countering that it is under no legal mandate to index external web pages under publishers' self-selected terms.What the ruling saidJudge Mehta rejected the claims that the search engine owed publishers guaranteed web traffic in return for crawling publicly accessible pages.“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free,” Mehta wrote.

passages: Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality.

SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground.
During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs).
Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive.
Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation.
WATCH: SpaceX launches its massive Starship rocket into orbit for first time

extraction.body: Google just made its boldest move yet into space-based computing, launching tensor processing units into orbit aboard Planet Labs satellites via SpaceX. The deployment marks a pivotal shift toward distributed AI infrastructure that could reshape how we think about cloud computing, bringing processing power directly to where data is collected in space. Google just sent its artificial intelligence capabilities literally into orbit, marking what industry experts are calling the dawn of space-based data centers. The tech giant's tensor processing units launched aboard Planet Labs satellites via a SpaceX mission, creating the first orbital deployment of enterprise AI chips designed for real-time space computing. Rather than beaming raw satellite data down to Earth for processing - a method that creates significant latency and bandwidth constraints - Google's orbital TPUs can now process information directly in space before transmitting refined results back to ground stations. Planet Labs, which operates the world's largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites, stands to benefit immediately from this arrangement. The company's satellites generate massive amounts of visual data daily, but current infrastructure requires downloading everything to Earth-based servers for AI analysis. With Google's TPUs now operating in orbit, that processing can happen in real-time as images are captured. Traditional satellite operations face a fundamental bottleneck - the limited bandwidth between space and ground stations. By processing data in orbit using Google's specialized AI chips, satellites can now perform complex analysis, identify patterns, and transmit only the most relevant information back to Earth. This could reduce data transmission requirements by orders of magnitude while dramatically improving response times for time-sensitive applications. SpaceX's role as the launch provider highlights how the commercial space industry is enabling new computing paradigms. The company's reliable and cost-effective launch capabilities have made it economically feasible to deploy sophisticated computing hardware in orbit, something that would have been prohibitively expensive just a decade ago. Amazon has been quietly developing its own space-based AWS infrastructure, while Microsoft has partnered with several satellite operators to test Azure services in orbit. Google's successful TPU deployment gives it a significant first-mover advantage in what's shaping up to be the next frontier of cloud computing. The orbital deployment of AI chips could enable entirely new categories of applications, from real-time climate monitoring to autonomous space traffic management. As satellite constellations grow larger and more sophisticated, the need for distributed processing power in space becomes increasingly critical. The company's TPUs, already proven in terrestrial data centers, are now pioneering the next evolution of distributed AI infrastructure. If successful, Google could deploy TPUs across multiple satellite constellations, creating a distributed AI network that spans the globe. Google's successful deployment of AI chips in orbit represents more than just a technical milestone - it's the opening move in what could become the most significant infrastructure shift since the advent of cloud computing. As more companies recognize the advantages of space-based processing, we're likely seeing the birth of an entirely new industry that combines the scale of cloud computing with the global reach of satellite networks. The race for orbital supremacy in AI processing has officially begun, and Google just took an early lead.

During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs).
Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive.
Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation.

The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident.
SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time.
The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025.
Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another.
Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion.

The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit.

extraction.body: Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality. The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident. SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time. SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground. During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs). The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025. The company aims to develop reliable, solar-powered AI computing infrastructure that can operate continuously in space. "Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected," Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher, wrote in a blog post following the launch. He called it the first step in a long-term research effort, "exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure." Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another. Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion. In low Earth orbit, satellites can "access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth," Alphabet said in the post. Eventually, they expect to be able to "link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit." The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit. SpaceX, led by Elon Musk , has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla , Musk's automaker. Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, "and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy "supercompute in space" in 2027. Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability. The Transporter-18 flight was the second major launch in a single day for SpaceX, which also began transporting astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida's Space Coast for NASA with an earlier liftoff on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit. sources.title: Google Launches AI Chips to Orbit in Space Data Center Push
passages: Google just sent its artificial intelligence capabilities literally into orbit, marking what industry experts are calling the dawn of space-based data centers.
By processing data in orbit using Google's specialized AI chips, satellites can now perform complex analysis, identify patterns, and transmit only the most relevant information back to Earth.

The tech giant's tensor processing units launched aboard Planet Labs satellites via a SpaceX mission, creating the first orbital deployment of enterprise AI chips designed for real-time space computing.

The deployment marks a pivotal shift toward distributed AI infrastructure that could reshape how we think about cloud computing, bringing processing power directly to where data is collected in space.
Amazon has been quietly developing its own space-based AWS infrastructure, while Microsoft has partnered with several satellite operators to test Azure services in orbit.
SpaceX's role as the launch provider highlights how the commercial space industry is enabling new computing paradigms.

extraction.body: Google just made its boldest move yet into space-based computing, launching tensor processing units into orbit aboard Planet Labs satellites via SpaceX. The deployment marks a pivotal shift toward distributed AI infrastructure that could reshape how we think about cloud computing, bringing processing power directly to where data is collected in space. Google just sent its artificial intelligence capabilities literally into orbit, marking what industry experts are calling the dawn of space-based data centers. The tech giant's tensor processing units launched aboard Planet Labs satellites via a SpaceX mission, creating the first orbital deployment of enterprise AI chips designed for real-time space computing. Rather than beaming raw satellite data down to Earth for processing - a method that creates significant latency and bandwidth constraints - Google's orbital TPUs can now process information directly in space before transmitting refined results back to ground stations. Planet Labs, which operates the world's largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites, stands to benefit immediately from this arrangement. The company's satellites generate massive amounts of visual data daily, but current infrastructure requires downloading everything to Earth-based servers for AI analysis. With Google's TPUs now operating in orbit, that processing can happen in real-time as images are captured. Traditional satellite operations face a fundamental bottleneck - the limited bandwidth between space and ground stations. By processing data in orbit using Google's specialized AI chips, satellites can now perform complex analysis, identify patterns, and transmit only the most relevant information back to Earth. This could reduce data transmission requirements by orders of magnitude while dramatically improving response times for time-sensitive applications. SpaceX's role as the launch provider highlights how the commercial space industry is enabling new computing paradigms. The company's reliable and cost-effective launch capabilities have made it economically feasible to deploy sophisticated computing hardware in orbit, something that would have been prohibitively expensive just a decade ago. Amazon has been quietly developing its own space-based AWS infrastructure, while Microsoft has partnered with several satellite operators to test Azure services in orbit. Google's successful TPU deployment gives it a significant first-mover advantage in what's shaping up to be the next frontier of cloud computing. The orbital deployment of AI chips could enable entirely new categories of applications, from real-time climate monitoring to autonomous space traffic management. As satellite constellations grow larger and more sophisticated, the need for distributed processing power in space becomes increasingly critical. The company's TPUs, already proven in terrestrial data centers, are now pioneering the next evolution of distributed AI infrastructure. If successful, Google could deploy TPUs across multiple satellite constellations, creating a distributed AI network that spans the globe. Google's successful deployment of AI chips in orbit represents more than just a technical milestone - it's the opening move in what could become the most significant infrastructure shift since the advent of cloud computing. As more companies recognize the advantages of space-based processing, we're likely seeing the birth of an entirely new industry that combines the scale of cloud computing with the global reach of satellite networks. The race for orbital supremacy in AI processing has officially begun, and Google just took an early lead.
