extraction.body: Source: Chip Somodevilla / Getty Welcome back for another edition of Surviving Trump, our round-up of the latest in President Donald Trump’s lies, corruption, and all-around Trump-foolery. Apparently, this is a series that would undoubtedly get NewsOne banned from the White House press corps, not because we’re lying about the lying-est president in recent history, but because Trump’s orangey-white supremacist butt gets hurt when the overwhelming majority of news outlets fail to report anything positive about him, which is pretty much always, and for the same reason virtually no media outlets would report anything positive about fire, brimstone, and flying locusts filling the skies. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about. Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication. Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot. 6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world. Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets. He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip. On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional. Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House. Trump is even out here touting Breitbart News — yes, that Breitbart News — as its beacon of truth and “the only outlet that covers him fairly.” Come on, y’all — this is a man who loves “fake news,” is “fake news,” and relies on “fake news” as his only political refuge. He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him. Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News. Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr. It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial. Speaking of AI, Trump’s love affair with AI slop continues to be an every-hour-on-the-hour thing, as do his self-revealed fantasies of global authoritarianism. In the image, the only nation clearly shown is Greenland, which likely means this post was inspired by the new Greenland deal he’s been boasting about, even though it’s the same deal we have had with the nation for 75 years, with a few more bells and whistles. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump claimed in a lengthy social media post. The U.S. has had a deal allowing it a largely unfettered military presence in Greenland since 1951, but the new deal is reportedly different because it makes U.S. military presence in the region permanent, according to Trump, and bars non-NATO nations from establishing their own presence in Greenland. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. He also didn’t seem to understand that calling his current term “THREE” undermined the message he was going for. On Friday, Trump posted what he called his “TOP 25 TRUMP ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF TERM THREE,” which included the termination of “scams” that only he has declared a scam, like the green energy efforts he has long declared war on, the “8 wars” he keeps claiming he ended without giving explicit examples, his National Guard deployments, which have largely been blocked by federal judges, including SCOTUS, because they’re unconstitutional, and the aforementioned drop in crime that he is in no way responsible for. Of course, Trump lying about his non-accomplishments is just par for the MAGA course, but his insistence that he’s actually served three terms because he still can’t handle his loss in 2020 should be a concern to anyone who wants to believe the nation isn’t being run by a poster child for mental health awareness for senior citizens. A CNN spokesperson told TheWrap: "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting.

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets.
When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news?

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," accusing the three news organizations of reporting "fake news" about him and his administration. "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social . "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." Asked about the ban during an Oval Office appearance later Friday, Trump said , "You need a free press. You need a fair press and an honest press. They purposely write negative news." The White House referred TheWrap to those remarks but did not clarify how the ban would be implemented or whether it would revoke reporters' credentials, restrict their access to the White House grounds or exclude the outlets from briefings, presidential events and the press pool. A CNN spokesperson told TheWrap: "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right." A Politico spokesperson said, "Politico will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them. The claims that Politico received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked." In his post, Trump falsely claimed that MSNBC changed its name to MS NOW "due to lack of viewership and credibility." The cable network rebranded in November 2025 because it was separating from NBCUniversal as part of Comcast's spinoff of Versant and could no longer use NBC's name and peacock logo. Versant said in a regulatory filing that the rebranding was announced "in connection with the Separation." Trump also described Politico as the recipient of an "illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription" from the federal government under former President Joe Biden. The figure referred to subscriptions purchased across government agencies, primarily for Politico Pro, the company's specialized policy-information service—not a single payment intended to keep the news organization operating. Both the Biden and Trump administrations paid for news-service subscriptions, according to a FactCheck.org review . The announcement marks Trump's latest escalation against news organizations whose coverage he opposes. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News.
Heinrich said that the Americans, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected in their coverage "regardless of whether government officials view it favorably".
"That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."
Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called Trump's White House ban illegal and unconstitutional.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.

It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.
Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Watch on Deadline The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool assignment for Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York. The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. CNN, Politico and MS NOW are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. The news outlets’ lawsuit was assigned to the same judge, Timothy J. Kelly, who presided over Acosta’s case. He set a hearing via videoconference for Wednesday, and set Tuesday as a deadline for the Trump response. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Boutrous said in a statement that the ban was a “direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process.” He added, “This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, Kelly ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets’ correspondents. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. extraction.body: Source: Chip Somodevilla / Getty Welcome back for another edition of Surviving Trump, our round-up of the latest in President Donald Trump’s lies, corruption, and all-around Trump-foolery. Apparently, this is a series that would undoubtedly get NewsOne banned from the White House press corps, not because we’re lying about the lying-est president in recent history, but because Trump’s orangey-white supremacist butt gets hurt when the overwhelming majority of news outlets fail to report anything positive about him, which is pretty much always, and for the same reason virtually no media outlets would report anything positive about fire, brimstone, and flying locusts filling the skies. Anyway, let’s get into it… Trump Defends White House Ban On CNN, MS NOW and Politico, As Outlets Sue Over 1st Amendment Attack The most annoying thing about Trump’s constant attacks on the free press, including his recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, is that he is so obviously and demonstrably the “fake news” he has spent the last decade complaining about. Look, all politicians lie, but Trump is in a league of his own when it comes to his reliance on propaganda as virtually his only mode of communication. Trump doesn’t just lie; he lies compulsively, and they’re consistently the most absurd, easily fact-checked lies told by any politician in any of our lifetimes, which, of course, is saying a lot. 6 — Trump’s entire existence as a U.S. president has been a 24/7, 365 detachment from any semblance of what’s going on in the real world. Since he announced the ban, Trump hasn’t once mentioned a specific grievance with any of the three outlets. He hasn’t mentioned a single lie they told about him; he’s only vaguely declared that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” And that hasn’t changed now that he’s claiming he is not attacking the free press; he also banned the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he posted on Truth Social on Monday. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Of course, that was after he told reporters in the White House that “the ban on the free press” was happening, which may or may not have been a Freudian slip. On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access to the White House, arguing that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” which could result in the federal courts stepping in, just as one did when the Pentagon tried to implement its own free speech-defying press policy, which virtually every mainstream media outlet — including conservative outlets like Newsmax and Fox News — responded to with a resounding “hell no,” leading to the policy being ruled unconstitutional. Speaking of Newsmax and Fox News, notice there’s no concern that those outlets, which have been successfully sued for peddling MAGA propaganda, might be banned from the White House. Trump is even out here touting Breitbart News — yes, that Breitbart News — as its beacon of truth and “the only outlet that covers him fairly.” Come on, y’all — this is a man who loves “fake news,” is “fake news,” and relies on “fake news” as his only political refuge. He’s just mad because media outlets won’t lie for him. Meanwhile, according to USA Today, major TV networks have decided to suspend their own White House pool coverage in protest of Trump’s ban, including ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — yes, that Fox News. Trump, the president who never met an expert he didn’t want to undermine in the name of MAGA science, responded by calling it all a big, all-caps-worthy “HOAX,” while fancying himself a “Hoax Buster.” Again, Mr. It would be the perfect example of Trump Intelligence, which is, if nothing else, artificial. Speaking of AI, Trump’s love affair with AI slop continues to be an every-hour-on-the-hour thing, as do his self-revealed fantasies of global authoritarianism. In the image, the only nation clearly shown is Greenland, which likely means this post was inspired by the new Greenland deal he’s been boasting about, even though it’s the same deal we have had with the nation for 75 years, with a few more bells and whistles. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns,” Trump claimed in a lengthy social media post. The U.S. has had a deal allowing it a largely unfettered military presence in Greenland since 1951, but the new deal is reportedly different because it makes U.S. military presence in the region permanent, according to Trump, and bars non-NATO nations from establishing their own presence in Greenland. Trump Still Thinks He’s Currently Serving A Third Term Earlier this year, Trump declared that “anybody running for President or Vice President should be forced to take a Cognitive Examination,” which seemed to be based on the fact that his own doctors keep making him take cognitive exams, which he doesn’t seem to know isn’t a thing that speaks to him being of sound mind. He also didn’t seem to understand that calling his current term “THREE” undermined the message he was going for. On Friday, Trump posted what he called his “TOP 25 TRUMP ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF TERM THREE,” which included the termination of “scams” that only he has declared a scam, like the green energy efforts he has long declared war on, the “8 wars” he keeps claiming he ended without giving explicit examples, his National Guard deployments, which have largely been blocked by federal judges, including SCOTUS, because they’re unconstitutional, and the aforementioned drop in crime that he is in no way responsible for. Of course, Trump lying about his non-accomplishments is just par for the MAGA course, but his insistence that he’s actually served three terms because he still can’t handle his loss in 2020 should be a concern to anyone who wants to believe the nation isn’t being run by a poster child for mental health awareness for senior citizens. The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites. However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law. The lawsuits were filed in 2025 , and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year. Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content. This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic. Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic . Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out. These arguments did not sway the judge, who noted that Google’s implicit agreement with websites is not legally relevant. “Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.” Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply. And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search. He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law . However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case. While Google is getting the dismissal it wanted, it doesn’t come away looking particularly good. Mehta recognizes that Google’s approach to AI search may be unfair to web publishers even if it’s not illegal. “The court does not treat Plaintiffs’ alleged harms lightly,” he wrote. “Nor is it unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in, and the knock-on consequences to journalists, educators, and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation.” This case essentially comes down to the nature of innovation. Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm. However, not all economic harm that may befall a company is the product of an illegal act. Mehta says that antitrust laws cannot be applied in place of legislative action just because something feels unfair: “The court is bound to apply the law only as it is written, not how the court or any party believes it ought to be.” Google will undoubtedly face more legal challenges over AI search, but it’s going to be an uphill battle in US courts absent new legislation, and lawmakers have been slow to adapt to the AI era. Publishers may have more luck overseas. The European Commission is currently considering these same questions, and it tends to take a dimmer view of Big Tech’s conduct. The UK has also ordered Google to provide an AI opt-out for sites that want to remain in organic search results. Google is exploring ways to pay sites directly for contributing to AI answers, but its pilot program is reportedly not going over well with publishers. It is simply how a general search engine works.”While Mehta noted he was not “unsympathetic to the situation of publishers and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation,” he held that antitrust statutes cannot serve as a stand-in for congressional action to remedy the economic fallout of technological innovation.You use AI every day.

coreStoryFacts.text: A federal judge has dismissed a pair of antitrust lawsuits filed by Chegg and Rolling Stone parent company Penske Media Corporation, which accused Google of driving away web traffic with its AI-powered search features, as reported earlier by Reuters.
This week, The Information reported that Google is paying around 100 publishers for their contributions to AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini as part of a pilot program.

It is simply how a general search engine works.” Mehta adds that the court is not “unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in,” but writes that antitrust rules can’t replace a legislative body’s decision to address the economic impact of “new innovation.” Meanwhile, publishers continue to see effects of Google’s AI-powered search overhaul, with traffic to news outlets and small websites taking a steep dive.
US District Judge Amit Mehta takes Google’s side in a ruling on Wednesday, writing that PMC and Chegg’s claims don’t stand up to antitrust law.
Judge Mehta, who made a landmark antitrust ruling against Google in 2024, disagrees with Chegg and PMC’s claims.
The publishers alleged Google’s practices diverted traffic away from their sites, hurting their revenue.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” Mehta writes.
In a setback for publishers worried about the effects of AI search, a US federal judge has dismissed lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google.
The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites.
However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.
The lawsuits were filed in 2025 , and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year.
Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content.
This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic.
Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic .
Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out.
Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply.
And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search.
He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law .
However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case.
The court acknowledges AI search comes with consequences, but it’s not an antitrust issue.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta.
Google is changing the way search operates, and that may come with economic harm.

sources.title: Elon Musk wants to put data centers in space — here's what that could actually look like - Yahoo Finance
passages: SpaceX ( SPAX.PVT ) founder Elon Musk has said that he wants to put data centers in space.
One industry founder told Yahoo Finance how it would actually work.

In its S-1 filing released Wednesday, SpaceX said its rockets and manufacturing expertise could power "massive AI compute satellite constellations — with potentially millions of satellites — for orbital data centers," with the first launch as early as 2028.
In the long term, "space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale," Elon Musk wrote in February when his startup XAI merged with SpaceX.

Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian contributed to this report.

"Imagine a big data center that's made out of Legos, and then you split those Lego bricks into all the individual bricks and have them fly in space right next to each other, and they all connect," Stott said.
Since August 2021, Lonestar has launched four test data center payloads into space — two to the International Space Station and two to the lunar surface.
In orbit, data centers can cast off their heat directly into the freezing vacuum of space without relying on air-cooling technologies, while the sun provides a continuous supply of energy.
" Now, once you build a space center, your biggest [operating expense] cost is gone."

One industry founder told Yahoo Finance how it would actually work. While the idea brings to mind massive buildings floating aimlessly through the cosmos, Christopher Stott, founder of Lonestar Data Holdings, a sovereign data storage company, told Yahoo Finance that the architecture of space-based computing is more akin to satellites orbiting in a tight, synchronized formation. "Imagine a big data center that's made out of Legos, and then you split those Lego bricks into all the individual bricks and have them fly in space right next to each other, and they all connect," Stott said. The connection is formed through optical lasers and radio frequencies. Lonestar is part of Nvidia's ( NVDA ) Inception program, which grants early-stage ventures access to AI chips and support so they can build and scale faster. Since August 2021, Lonestar has launched four test data center payloads into space — two to the International Space Station and two to the lunar surface. Lonestar customers include governments, NGOs, and social media companies. The biggest incentive to scale AI data centers in space is cost, Stott explained. In orbit, data centers can cast off their heat directly into the freezing vacuum of space without relying on air-cooling technologies, while the sun provides a continuous supply of energy. "Energy is so expensive," he said. " Now, once you build a space center, your biggest [operating expense] cost is gone." Multiple companies are trying to make the vision of data centers in space a reality. In its S-1 filing released Wednesday, SpaceX said its rockets and manufacturing expertise could power "massive AI compute satellite constellations — with potentially millions of satellites — for orbital data centers," with the first launch as early as 2028. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that Alphabet's Google ( GOOG ) and SpaceX are in advanced discussions over launching data centers in space. Last year, Google announced Project Suncatcher , a moonshot initiative aimed at launching prototype satellites by 2027. The company is working with Planet Labs to build those satellites. A partnership with SpaceX would enhance those aspirations, with SpaceX being the preeminent private rocket launch company and space payload provider, the Journal said. In the long term, "space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale," Elon Musk wrote in February when his startup XAI merged with SpaceX. "The only logical solution therefore is to transport these resource-intensive efforts to a location with vast power and space," he added. Execution may include some challenges. Two of the payloads launched by Lonestar tipped over when they landed on the surface of the moon. However, Stott said the company finished testing one of them in lunar orbit prior to landing. The other one kept running even after it tipped over. "It was still running," said Stott. "The servers didn't need to be right-side-up to process data," he said. It's unclear what the timeline is for putting data centers in space. Musk told Forbes in an interview earlier this month that "data centers in space is much easier than people may think." Blue Origin, founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, recently announced TeraWave, a proposed network of thousands of laser-linked satellites designed to handle massive enterprise data traffic from orbit. In an interview with CNBC on Wednesday , Bezos said the reality of running data centers in space "will happen," though he doesn't know how long it will take. "Some of the timelines we hear are very short. They're probably not right," said Bezos. Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian contributed to this report. sources.title: SpaceX launches Google AI chips into orbit in push toward space-based data centers - CNBC
passages: Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality.

SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground.
During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs).
Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive.
Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation.
WATCH: SpaceX launches its massive Starship rocket into orbit for first time
The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident.
SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time.
The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025.
Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another.
Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion.

The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit.

extraction.body: Alphabet launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit on Thursday in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, a step towards making data centers in space a reality. The launch window opened at 11:15 am PT from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California's Santa Barbara County, with liftoff occurring without incident. SpaceX successfully deployed all payloads on board by 1 p.m. local time. SpaceX has promoted supercomputers in space as the next frontier in artificial intelligence infrastructure, touting "infinite real estate" in orbit as a means of escaping the data center backlash on the ground. During the uncrewed Transporter-18 mission, SpaceX will carry Planet Labs satellites, including a solar-powered prototype equipped with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs). The Thursday launch marks the first in-orbit test for Alphabet's Project Suncatcher, a "moonshot" initiative Google first revealed in November 2025. The company aims to develop reliable, solar-powered AI computing infrastructure that can operate continuously in space. "Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected," Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher, wrote in a blog post following the launch. He called it the first step in a long-term research effort, "exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure." Alphabet is a significant investor in SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO, and the businesses are close partners even as their AI divisions compete with one another. Alphabet's stake in SpaceX is currently valued at over $82 billion. In low Earth orbit, satellites can "access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth," Alphabet said in the post. Eventually, they expect to be able to "link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit." The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit. SpaceX, led by Elon Musk , has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla , Musk's automaker. Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, "and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy "supercompute in space" in 2027. Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability. The Transporter-18 flight was the second major launch in a single day for SpaceX, which also began transporting astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida's Space Coast for NASA with an earlier liftoff on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit. Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, “and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest.” SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy “supercompute in space” in 2027.

Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability.

The Transporter-18 flight will be the second potentially historic launch in a single day for SpaceX, which is also slated to carry astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida’s Space Coast for NASA on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit.

extraction.body: Google just made its boldest move yet into space-based computing, launching tensor processing units into orbit aboard Planet Labs satellites via SpaceX. The deployment marks a pivotal shift toward distributed AI infrastructure that could reshape how we think about cloud computing, bringing processing power directly to where data is collected in space. Google just sent its artificial intelligence capabilities literally into orbit, marking what industry experts are calling the dawn of space-based data centers. The tech giant's tensor processing units launched aboard Planet Labs satellites via a SpaceX mission, creating the first orbital deployment of enterprise AI chips designed for real-time space computing. Rather than beaming raw satellite data down to Earth for processing - a method that creates significant latency and bandwidth constraints - Google's orbital TPUs can now process information directly in space before transmitting refined results back to ground stations. Planet Labs, which operates the world's largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites, stands to benefit immediately from this arrangement. The company's satellites generate massive amounts of visual data daily, but current infrastructure requires downloading everything to Earth-based servers for AI analysis. With Google's TPUs now operating in orbit, that processing can happen in real-time as images are captured. Traditional satellite operations face a fundamental bottleneck - the limited bandwidth between space and ground stations. By processing data in orbit using Google's specialized AI chips, satellites can now perform complex analysis, identify patterns, and transmit only the most relevant information back to Earth. This could reduce data transmission requirements by orders of magnitude while dramatically improving response times for time-sensitive applications. SpaceX's role as the launch provider highlights how the commercial space industry is enabling new computing paradigms. The company's reliable and cost-effective launch capabilities have made it economically feasible to deploy sophisticated computing hardware in orbit, something that would have been prohibitively expensive just a decade ago. Amazon has been quietly developing its own space-based AWS infrastructure, while Microsoft has partnered with several satellite operators to test Azure services in orbit. Google's successful TPU deployment gives it a significant first-mover advantage in what's shaping up to be the next frontier of cloud computing. The orbital deployment of AI chips could enable entirely new categories of applications, from real-time climate monitoring to autonomous space traffic management. As satellite constellations grow larger and more sophisticated, the need for distributed processing power in space becomes increasingly critical. The company's TPUs, already proven in terrestrial data centers, are now pioneering the next evolution of distributed AI infrastructure. If successful, Google could deploy TPUs across multiple satellite constellations, creating a distributed AI network that spans the globe. Google's successful deployment of AI chips in orbit represents more than just a technical milestone - it's the opening move in what could become the most significant infrastructure shift since the advent of cloud computing. As more companies recognize the advantages of space-based processing, we're likely seeing the birth of an entirely new industry that combines the scale of cloud computing with the global reach of satellite networks. The race for orbital supremacy in AI processing has officially begun, and Google just took an early lead.

The company aims to develop reliable, solar-powered AI computing infrastructure that can operate continuously in space. "Our team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected," Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher, wrote in a blog post following the launch. The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn't yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit. SpaceX, led by Elon Musk , has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla , Musk's automaker. Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, "and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy "supercompute in space" in 2027. Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability. The Transporter-18 flight was the second major launch in a single day for SpaceX, which also began transporting astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida's Space Coast for NASA with an earlier liftoff on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit. In low Earth orbit, satellites can “access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth,” Alphabet said in the post. Eventually, they expect to be able to “link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit.”

The Google parent has already tested its TPUs running AI workloads in a facility at the University of California at Davis, but doesn’t yet know how its chips will perform in the challenging conditions of low Earth orbit.

SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, has also announced that it plans to build and launch its own orbital data centers. They will be comprised of swarms of satellites the company develops in Redmond, Washington, equipped with graphics processing units and solar arrays it plans to produce with Tesla, Musk’s automaker.

Earlier this year, Musk said data centers in space would be the cheapest way to train AI, “and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest.” SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said at an event in September that the company will deploy “supercompute in space” in 2027.

Industry experts say space-based data centers represent a far-out mission, if they can even become feasible, in part because rocket launches remain capacity-constrained and expensive. Orbital data centers would also require cooling systems and chips that can withstand extreme temperatures, as well as protection from radiation. Clutter and orbital debris could also impede their viability.

The Transporter-18 flight will be the second potentially historic launch in a single day for SpaceX, which is also slated to carry astronauts to the International Space Station from Florida’s Space Coast for NASA on Thursday, marking the start of a six-month mission in orbit.

extraction.body: Google just made its boldest move yet into space-based computing, launching tensor processing units into orbit aboard Planet Labs satellites via SpaceX. The deployment marks a pivotal shift toward distributed AI infrastructure that could reshape how we think about cloud computing, bringing processing power directly to where data is collected in space. Google just sent its artificial intelligence capabilities literally into orbit, marking what industry experts are calling the dawn of space-based data centers. The tech giant's tensor processing units launched aboard Planet Labs satellites via a SpaceX mission, creating the first orbital deployment of enterprise AI chips designed for real-time space computing. Rather than beaming raw satellite data down to Earth for processing - a method that creates significant latency and bandwidth constraints - Google's orbital TPUs can now process information directly in space before transmitting refined results back to ground stations. Planet Labs, which operates the world's largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites, stands to benefit immediately from this arrangement. The company's satellites generate massive amounts of visual data daily, but current infrastructure requires downloading everything to Earth-based servers for AI analysis. With Google's TPUs now operating in orbit, that processing can happen in real-time as images are captured. Traditional satellite operations face a fundamental bottleneck - the limited bandwidth between space and ground stations. By processing data in orbit using Google's specialized AI chips, satellites can now perform complex analysis, identify patterns, and transmit only the most relevant information back to Earth. This could reduce data transmission requirements by orders of magnitude while dramatically improving response times for time-sensitive applications. SpaceX's role as the launch provider highlights how the commercial space industry is enabling new computing paradigms. The company's reliable and cost-effective launch capabilities have made it economically feasible to deploy sophisticated computing hardware in orbit, something that would have been prohibitively expensive just a decade ago. Amazon has been quietly developing its own space-based AWS infrastructure, while Microsoft has partnered with several satellite operators to test Azure services in orbit. Google's successful TPU deployment gives it a significant first-mover advantage in what's shaping up to be the next frontier of cloud computing. The orbital deployment of AI chips could enable entirely new categories of applications, from real-time climate monitoring to autonomous space traffic management. As satellite constellations grow larger and more sophisticated, the need for distributed processing power in space becomes increasingly critical. The company's TPUs, already proven in terrestrial data centers, are now pioneering the next evolution of distributed AI infrastructure. If successful, Google could deploy TPUs across multiple satellite constellations, creating a distributed AI network that spans the globe. Google's successful deployment of AI chips in orbit represents more than just a technical milestone - it's the opening move in what could become the most significant infrastructure shift since the advent of cloud computing. As more companies recognize the advantages of space-based processing, we're likely seeing the birth of an entirely new industry that combines the scale of cloud computing with the global reach of satellite networks. The race for orbital supremacy in AI processing has officially begun, and Google just took an early lead.

passages: Anthropic has signed an agreement with Google and Broadcom for approximately 3.5 gigawatts of computing capacity built on Google's tensor processing units, with the capacity expected to come online starting in 2027, the company said Monday.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said during an earnings call last month that Broadcom was providing one gigawatt of Google TPU compute for Anthropic this year, according to CNBC .
Broadcom stock gained as much as 3.6% in after-hours trading following the news.
No financial terms were attached to the agreement.

According to Monday's securities filing, Broadcom flagged that Anthropic's ability to draw on the additional compute hinges on its ongoing commercial performance, and noted that discussions with outside operational and financial partners are underway to support the rollout.
Anthropic has warned the label could cost it billions in lost revenue.
Still, the company's annualized revenue has more than tripled in recent months, driven in part by demand for its Claude Code developer tools and broader enterprise adoption.

Anthropic also said Monday that its revenue run rate has now crossed $30 billion on an annualized basis — more than three times the roughly $9 billion figure it recorded at the ende of 2025.

Enterprise traction has also accelerated: The number of clients committing at least $1 million a year has surpassed 1,000, a threshold Anthropic said is twice what it was reporting around the time of its Series G announcement in February.

Anthropic trains and runs its Claude models across multiple hardware platforms — including AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, and Nvidia GPUs — and describes Amazon Web Services as its primary cloud and training partner.
Claude is available on AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Azure Foundry.

extraction.body: Anthropic's IPO prospectus documents extensive partnerships with a handful of big tech firms. One stands out: chip maker Broadcom . The company's relationship with Anthropic spans compute supply, equipment ⁠leasing and financing -- giving the semiconductor company a central role in Anthropic's infrastructure buildout. That differentiates it from other major partners and investors ​such as Amazon , which primarily provide ​cloud infrastructure and distribution for ​Anthropic's model Claude. As part of that complex relationship, revealed in the IPO filing, Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to finance infrastructure spending. In turn, Anthropic stands to become the largest customer in Broadcom's bread-and-butter chip design business next year, making their ⁠relationship a ‌prime example of the reciprocal spending that has animated AI ⁠skeptics on Wall Street, even as the AI lab readies a public offering that could see it valued at $2 trillion. "It feels that there's quite a concentrated bet right now on two companies being able to generate enough revenues to support all the financing that's happened," said ‌Robert Leitao, managing partner of Rothschild & Co. As part of the financing arrangement, Broadcom could designate a financing partner, and the debt instruments could be converted into Anthropic shares. Anthropic said in its filing it doesn't expect ​any notes to be sold before it completes its IPO. The convertible note Anthropic would issue could finance about a third of the $125.2 billion commitment the AI lab has made for a five-year lease of tensor processing unit (TPU) computing capacity. Anthropic announced ⁠in April an expanded partnership with Broadcom and Google that will give it access to multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU compute capacity ‌beginning in 2027. "Nvidia is putting in place a massive amount of its balance sheet, and Broadcom is having to follow suit," Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg said. Anthropic disclosed that ⁠Broadcom's role in supplying hardware and acting as a financing partner creates "potential conflicts of interest" that might ⁠affect Anthropic's ability to access the computing power needed for its work, according to the prospectus. The ⁠AI lab also warned that Broadcom's decisions around pricing and hardware could affect its ability to procure enough computing infrastructure. Broadcom did not comment. Anthropic declined to comment. The company warned that certain payment or performance defaults could make a substantial portion of its lease obligations immediately due while limiting its ability to use the $42 billion financing facility to cover those payments. passages: Anthropic's IPO filing reveals Broadcom has agreed to lend the AI lab up to $42 billion in convertible notes, covering roughly a third of its $125.2 billion five-year TPU lease commitment.
Buried in the prospectus Anthropic filed toward its public listing is a number that reframes its entire relationship with one of its biggest suppliers.
That blurs the line between vendor and creditor right as Wall Street tries to price the company.
Frankly, this is the same circularity that's defined AI financing all year, just with a new name attached.
Nvidia committed up to $100 billion to OpenAI while also selling it the chips that money would buy.
In November, Microsoft and Nvidia together put as much as $15 billion into Anthropic.
That was part of a deal where Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion of Azure compute running on Nvidia systems, a round that valued Anthropic around $350 billion, according to CNBC.

Broadcom's $42 billion facility follows the identical shape: the supplier finances the customer so the customer can keep buying from the supplier, and the revenue shows up on both companies' books as real growth.
Anthropic's own prospectus flags the problem.
The filing warns that a payment or performance default could make a large share of its lease obligations due immediately.
In plain terms, the backstop is least available exactly when it's needed most.
Anthropic also disclosed it had already deposited restricted cash into an account for Broadcom back in April, with room for more deposits to come.
The filing says Anthropic doesn't expect any of the notes to actually be sold before the IPO closes.
What makes the Broadcom version sharper is the scale next to Anthropic's actual business.
Anthropic brought in close to $4.6 billion in revenue last year and lost more than $8 billion doing it.
It's now carrying roughly $518 billion in total infrastructure obligations stretching out over the coming years.
A $42 billion credit line sounds enormous until you set it beside that number, where it covers a slice of a slice.
The stock is still sitting 27% below its June high of $481.57, even with Wall Street's average price target near $532.
Broadcom projects about $115 billion in AI revenue by 2027 and $230 billion by 2028, with Anthropic becoming its largest compute customer that year.

Broadcom's residual value support could turn custom chips into a repeatable asset-backed finance model. - how Anthropic finances AI chip infrastructure costs - Wall Street structured credit for AI compute capacity
Apollo and Blackstone raised $35 billion in June to finance Google chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping the senior tranches of that debt, according to reporting at the time.
Broadcom doesn't make TPUs outright, it co-designs them with Google, then layers on a role as lessor and now as lender for the capacity Anthropic is leasing.

extraction.body: Anthropic's IPO filing reveals Broadcom has agreed to lend the AI lab up to $42 billion in convertible notes, covering roughly a third of its $125.2 billion five-year TPU lease commitment. The arrangement ties Broadcom's balance sheet directly to Anthropic's compute buildout just as the company heads toward a public listing. Anthropic's IPO filing shows Broadcom isn't just selling the AI lab chips, it's agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to help pay for them. That blurs the line between vendor and creditor right as Wall Street tries to price the company. Buried in the prospectus Anthropic filed toward its public listing is a number that reframes its entire relationship with one of its biggest suppliers. Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic as much as $42 billion through convertible notes, according to Reuters, which first reported the filing's details. Anthropic has made a $125.2 billion, five-year commitment for tensor processing unit computing capacity. The loan is meant to help cover it, which means it handles roughly a third of what Anthropic already owes for the compute it's renting. Here's the twist. The chips themselves are Google's. Broadcom doesn't make TPUs outright, it co-designs them with Google, then layers on a role as lessor and now as lender for the capacity Anthropic is leasing. So Broadcom is simultaneously a hardware partner, a landlord for compute, and a bank: three jobs that don't usually sit inside one company's relationship with a single customer. Anthropic's own prospectus flags the problem. The filing warns that a payment or performance default could make a large share of its lease obligations due immediately. At the very same time, it could limit Anthropic's ability to draw on the $42 billion facility to cover them. In plain terms, the backstop is least available exactly when it's needed most. Anthropic also disclosed it had already deposited restricted cash into an account for Broadcom back in April, with room for more deposits to come. The filing says Anthropic doesn't expect any of the notes to actually be sold before the IPO closes. Frankly, this is the same circularity that's defined AI financing all year, just with a new name attached. Nvidia committed up to $100 billion to OpenAI while also selling it the chips that money would buy. In November, Microsoft and Nvidia together put as much as $15 billion into Anthropic. That was part of a deal where Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion of Azure compute running on Nvidia systems, a round that valued Anthropic around $350 billion, according to CNBC. Broadcom's $42 billion facility follows the identical shape: the supplier finances the customer so the customer can keep buying from the supplier, and the revenue shows up on both companies' books as real growth. Apollo and Blackstone's $35 billion financing for Anthropic shows how AI compute is becoming a private credit asset, not just a venture capital expense. The deal also highlights how Anthropic is building a different capital strategy as OpenAI moves toward a public listing. - how to finance AI infrastructure with private credit - private credit deals for semiconductor and chip investments What makes the Broadcom version sharper is the scale next to Anthropic's actual business. Anthropic brought in close to $4.6 billion in revenue last year and lost more than $8 billion doing it. It's now carrying roughly $518 billion in total infrastructure obligations stretching out over the coming years. A $42 billion credit line sounds enormous until you set it beside that number, where it covers a slice of a slice. Broadcom projects about $115 billion in AI revenue by 2027 and $230 billion by 2028, with Anthropic becoming its largest compute customer that year. It isn't the first time Broadcom has backed this kind of arrangement either. Apollo and Blackstone raised $35 billion in June to finance Google chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping the senior tranches of that debt, according to reporting at the time. The Anthropic facility is the same instinct applied directly to Broadcom's own customer relationship instead of a third party's. Markets shrugged. Broadcom shares closed Tuesday at $351.19, down about 1%, and ticked up less than half a percent in Wednesday premarket trading, nowhere near the reaction you'd expect for a $42 billion commitment. The stock is still sitting 27% below its June high of $481.57, even with Wall Street's average price target near $532. None of this means the arrangement is fraudulent or even unusual for this stage of the AI buildout. It means the people actually carrying the risk on Anthropic's compute bet are not just its venture investors, they're the chipmaker selling it the hardware and now lending it the cash to pay for that hardware too. When a company's biggest vendor becomes its biggest creditor on the eve of a public listing, that's not a financing footnote. That's the balance sheet talking, and prospective shareholders would do well to listen to what it's actually saying. Broadcom projects about $115 billion in AI revenue by 2027 and $230 billion by 2028, with Anthropic becoming its largest compute customer that year.

It isn't the first time Broadcom has backed this kind of arrangement either. Apollo and Blackstone raised $35 billion in June to finance Google chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping the senior tranches of that debt, according to reporting at the time. Markets shrugged. Broadcom shares closed Tuesday at $351.19, down about 1%, and ticked up less than half a percent in Wednesday premarket trading, nowhere near the reaction you'd expect for a $42 billion commitment. passages: The mechanics are narrower than the headline.
The instruments Anthropic would issue are convertible into Anthropic shares.
Anthropic deposited cash into a restricted account for Broadcom’s benefit in April 2026 and may have to add more.
The company also warned that a payment or performance default could make a substantial share of the lease obligations due at once, and could block use of the $42 billion facility to pay them.
A backstop that disappears in the scenario it was written for is a different instrument from a committed loan.

In June, Apollo and Blackstone raised $35 billion to finance Anthropic’s lease of Google chips that Broadcom helps develop, aimed first at about a gigawatt and, as a partnership, at as much as 20 gigawatts through 2028, the Financial Times reported .
Broadcom backstopped interest on the two senior tranches.
In August, Bloomberg, via Reuters , said a further Broadcom-linked debt talk could run past $60 billion.
Today’s $42 billion is the prospectus ceiling.
It is neither the June loan nor that August discussion.
Three different $40-billion-scale numbers are now in circulation.

Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion so the lab can lease tensor-processing-unit capacity, a commitment sitting in Anthropic’s IPO filing and reported by Reuters on October 1, 2026 .
On that news, Nasdaq had Broadcom at $352.25 at 8:49 a.m.
ET, up $1.06, or 0.30%, from Wednesday’s $351.19 close.
A facility sized to about a third of a $125.2 billion, five-year TPU lease moved the stock 0.30%.
Mizuho’s Vijay Rakesh, in a note CNBC cited that week, estimated Broadcom would take in $21 billion of AI revenue from Anthropic in 2026 and $42 billion in 2027.
The April announcement itself carried no dollar figure.
The other is an undrawn, multi-year loan cap against a lease.
They share a number, and that is the point skeptics have reached for.
If the revenue hope and the credit ceiling are the same size, the customer’s ability to pay and the vendor’s willingness to lend are no longer independent facts.
The stock already sits 27% under its June 2 closing high of $481.57 because the customer was already inside the guide.

In September Broadcom put AI semiconductor revenue at about $115 billion for fiscal 2027 and about $230 billion for fiscal 2028, and Reuters reported with today’s filing that Anthropic is expected to be the largest compute customer in 2027.
The incremental fact is who writes the cheque.
Equipment vendors did this with telecom carriers into 2000.
About 80% of the $518 billion buildout, on the September prospectus reporting, is non-cancellable or payable whether the capacity is used.
This lease is one more obligation that does not shrink when demand does.
Anthropic’s 2025 revenue was nearly $4.6 billion, against operating losses above $8 billion and a lease stack in the hundreds of billions.
The 0.30% premarket gain prices a $42 billion option as an option.
The move that would actually change AVGO is already on the Street: a $531.85 average target, 51% above $351.19, from 50 analysts on MarketScreener .
A facility that funds a lease the guide already counted will not re-rate AVGO.

The arrangement ties Broadcom's balance sheet directly to Anthropic's compute buildout just as the company heads toward a public listing. Buried in the prospectus Anthropic filed toward its public listing is a number that reframes its entire relationship with one of its biggest suppliers. Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic as much as $42 billion through convertible notes, according to Reuters, which first reported the filing's details. Anthropic has made a $125.2 billion, five-year commitment for tensor processing unit computing capacity. The loan is meant to help cover it, which means it handles roughly a third of what Anthropic already owes for the compute it's renting. Here's the twist. The chips themselves are Google's. Broadcom doesn't make TPUs outright, it co-designs them with Google, then layers on a role as lessor and now as lender for the capacity Anthropic is leasing. So Broadcom is simultaneously a hardware partner, a landlord for compute, and a bank: three jobs that don't usually sit inside one company's relationship with a single customer. Anthropic's own prospectus flags the problem. The filing warns that a payment or performance default could make a large share of its lease obligations due immediately. At the very same time, it could limit Anthropic's ability to draw on the $42 billion facility to cover them. In plain terms, the backstop is least available exactly when it's needed most. Anthropic also disclosed it had already deposited restricted cash into an account for Broadcom back in April, with room for more deposits to come. The filing says Anthropic doesn't expect any of the notes to actually be sold before the IPO closes. Frankly, this is the same circularity that's defined AI financing all year, just with a new name attached. Broadcom's $42 billion facility follows the identical shape: the supplier finances the customer so the customer can keep buying from the supplier, and the revenue shows up on both companies' books as real growth. Apollo and Blackstone's $35 billion financing for Anthropic shows how AI compute is becoming a private credit asset, not just a venture capital expense. The deal also highlights how Anthropic is building a different capital strategy as OpenAI moves toward a public listing. - how to finance AI infrastructure with private credit - private credit deals for semiconductor and chip investments What makes the Broadcom version sharper is the scale next to Anthropic's actual business. It's now carrying roughly $518 billion in total infrastructure obligations stretching out over the coming years. A $42 billion credit line sounds enormous until you set it beside that number, where it covers a slice of a slice. Broadcom projects about $115 billion in AI revenue by 2027 and $230 billion by 2028, with Anthropic becoming its largest compute customer that year. It isn't the first time Broadcom has backed this kind of arrangement either. Apollo and Blackstone raised $35 billion in June to finance Google chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping the senior tranches of that debt, according to reporting at the time. The Anthropic facility is the same instinct applied directly to Broadcom's own customer relationship instead of a third party's. Markets shrugged. Broadcom shares closed Tuesday at $351.19, down about 1%, and ticked up less than half a percent in Wednesday premarket trading, nowhere near the reaction you'd expect for a $42 billion commitment. The stock is still sitting 27% below its June high of $481.57, even with Wall Street's average price target near $532. It means the people actually carrying the risk on Anthropic's compute bet are not just its venture investors, they're the chipmaker selling it the hardware and now lending it the cash to pay for that hardware too. When a company's biggest vendor becomes its biggest creditor on the eve of a public listing, that's not a financing footnote. That's the balance sheet talking, and prospective shareholders would do well to listen to what it's actually saying. A backstop that disappears in the scenario it was written for is a different instrument from a committed loan.

Broadcom backstopped interest on the two senior tranches.
In August, Bloomberg, via Reuters , said a further Broadcom-linked debt talk could run past $60 billion.
Today’s $42 billion is the prospectus ceiling.
It is neither the June loan nor that August discussion.
Three different $40-billion-scale numbers are now in circulation.

Broadcom has agreed to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion so the lab can lease tensor-processing-unit capacity, a commitment sitting in Anthropic’s IPO filing and reported by Reuters on October 1, 2026 .
On that news, Nasdaq had Broadcom at $352.25 at 8:49 a.m.
ET, up $1.06, or 0.30%, from Wednesday’s $351.19 close.
A facility sized to about a third of a $125.2 billion, five-year TPU lease moved the stock 0.30%.
Mizuho’s Vijay Rakesh, in a note CNBC cited that week, estimated Broadcom would take in $21 billion of AI revenue from Anthropic in 2026 and $42 billion in 2027.
The April announcement itself carried no dollar figure.
The other is an undrawn, multi-year loan cap against a lease.
They share a number, and that is the point skeptics have reached for.
If the revenue hope and the credit ceiling are the same size, the customer’s ability to pay and the vendor’s willingness to lend are no longer independent facts.
The stock already sits 27% under its June 2 closing high of $481.57 because the customer was already inside the guide.

In September Broadcom put AI semiconductor revenue at about $115 billion for fiscal 2027 and about $230 billion for fiscal 2028, and Reuters reported with today’s filing that Anthropic is expected to be the largest compute customer in 2027.
The incremental fact is who writes the cheque.
Equipment vendors did this with telecom carriers into 2000.
About 80% of the $518 billion buildout, on the September prospectus reporting, is non-cancellable or payable whether the capacity is used.
This lease is one more obligation that does not shrink when demand does.
Anthropic’s 2025 revenue was nearly $4.6 billion, against operating losses above $8 billion and a lease stack in the hundreds of billions.
The 0.30% premarket gain prices a $42 billion option as an option.
The move that would actually change AVGO is already on the Street: a $531.85 average target, 51% above $351.19, from 50 analysts on MarketScreener .
A facility that funds a lease the guide already counted will not re-rate AVGO.
Alphabet’s Google and Broadcom have collaborated on several generations of those TPUs.
Anthropic said in April that an expanded partnership would give it multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity beginning in 2027.

The wider Anthropic math, from Reuters on September 29 , is what the ceiling is being asked to sit under.
Two customers each accounted for 12% of revenue, and 47% of sales ran through Amazon’s and Google’s cloud marketplaces.
FinanceFeeds set out what that ask implies per share in the September 30 IPO price piece .
The lab is short-dated on revenue and long-dated on cost.
A convertible that can make Broadcom a shareholder adds a related party to a register that already includes the cloud vendors.
Reuters’ September reading put their marketplace fee near 16 cents per dollar of those sales.
The new information is the cap, the convertibility and the conflict language, and those wait on a public conversion price.
Hock Tan’s April line remains the last detailed public description of this customer, and it was a volume statement, not a promise to advance $42 billion.

passages: LONDON — Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
sources.body: LONDON — Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.

extraction.body: LONDON — Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran. The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement. A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police “under caution,” which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions. On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said the investigation “is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry. “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement,” she said. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident. The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran. Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant five suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move. Burnham said authorities have the investigation under “the strongest grip and the closest control,” and British officials had been “talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done.” U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

On Sunday, five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested over the incident at RAF Fairford, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.

extraction.body: LONDON (AP) — British police have arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run air base on the weekend. The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital. On Sunday, five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested over the incident at RAF Fairford, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. They have since been released on bail. Counter-terror police said a second man, a 26-year-old U.K. national, has also been questioned under caution. “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement,” the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing for the Metropolitan Police, Vicki Evans, said. “I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation.” © 2026 WTOP, LLC.
