sources.title: Sanchez demands UN Security Council reform, abolition of permanent veto and condemns Gaza genocide
passages: Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, Sanchez insisted that the international governing architecture must adapt to reflect current realities: "We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members."

Highlighting Spain's foreign policy actions, Sanchez cited sanctions against Russia and Madrid's arms embargo on the Israeli government, reaffirming an "unequivocal" condemnation of the "genocide that Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza."

Sanchez denounced what he characterised as a "planned and coordinated demolition attempt" directed at weakening multilateral institutions: "They start by questioning the rules, then they break them, knowing well that nobody will dare to hold them accountable.
They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies like this one.

Addressing migration in the North African enclave of Ceuta, where roughly 72,000 people crossed irregularly in late July, Sanchez pledged Spain will respect human rights rather than "turn migrants into the enemy."

extraction.body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for an overhaul of the United Nations Security Council to guarantee equitable representation across all regions and to abolish the permanent veto power wielded by its five permanent members. Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, Sanchez insisted that the international governing architecture must adapt to reflect current realities: "We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members." Sanchez argued that under the principles of the UN Charter, "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are." He cautioned that fundamental pillars — peace, sustainability, and equal opportunity —are facing systematic assaults from political actors seeking to drag the world back into a "dark past." Highlighting Spain's foreign policy actions, Sanchez cited sanctions against Russia and Madrid's arms embargo on the Israeli government, reaffirming an "unequivocal" condemnation of the "genocide that Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza." Sanchez denounced what he characterised as a "planned and coordinated demolition attempt" directed at weakening multilateral institutions: "They start by questioning the rules, then they break them, knowing well that nobody will dare to hold them accountable. They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies like this one. They obstruct these organisations' ability to act, so then write them off as useless entities that we can do without." Despite these challenges, he urged member states to rebuild trust in the UN. Turning to succession, Sanchez insisted the next secretary-general should be a Latin American woman — noting that all nine postholders to date have been men — describing it as a "historic debt that we must settle." Addressing migration in the North African enclave of Ceuta, where roughly 72,000 people crossed irregularly in late July, Sanchez pledged Spain will respect human rights rather than "turn migrants into the enemy."

extraction.body: The General Assembly met on Thursday to examine the Security Council’s latest veto , cast by China and Russia over a United States-backed sanctions panel of experts on Iran nuclear facilities. Many nations have called for removing or limiting veto power in the Council, but reform of the 15-member organ remains a work in progress. At last year’s annual veto debate, then-General Assembly president Annalena Baerbock called repeated veto use a “ poster child ” for global gridlock. Thursday’s debate was triggered by the assembly’s landmark veto initiative, established in 2022. Khalilur Rahman, president of the assembly’s 81st session, said the veto initiative “cannot substitute for effective Security Council action”. Each invocation of the initiative “ highlights both the value of this mechanism and the circumstances that make it necessary ” and affirms the assembly’s complementary role, ensuring that veto use is accompanied by transparency, explanation and consideration by the wider membership. While the initiative does not override the veto, it guarantees a public and accountable debate on each use and its implications in the General Assembly, where there is no veto power. During the debate, Deputy Permanent Representative Sun Lei of China said that his delegation voted against the draft resolution to “uphold a correct sense of right and wrong”. The current impasse on the sanctions panel arises from the United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action on Iran’s nuclear facilities – the Iran nuclear deal of 2015 – its campaign of “maximum pressure” and its “two rounds of strikes against Iran in the midst of negotiations”. Meanwhile, other delegates argued for extending the panel’s mandate. “No UN Member State should prevent the UN Security Council from functioning properly and being fully operational,” said Hedda Samson, Deputy Head of the European Union delegation, noting that the need for a panel of experts is “even great today”. Following Thursday’s debate, the assembly president will send a summary of discussions back to the Security Council. At the outset of the meeting, Mr. Rahman said the assembly and the council “serve humanity best when they operate in balance”, each fulfilling its distinct but complementary responsibilities under the UN Charter . “ Let us, therefore, use this debate not to exacerbate tensions or assign blame, but to clarify positions, identify common ground for constructive solutions and chart a credible path forward to support dialogue and diplomacy and ultimately restore trust in the organization and its ability to deliver,” he said. extraction.body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for an overhaul of the United Nations Security Council to guarantee equitable representation across all regions and to abolish the permanent veto power wielded by its five permanent members. Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, Sanchez insisted that the international governing architecture must adapt to reflect current realities: "We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members." Sanchez argued that under the principles of the UN Charter, "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are." He cautioned that fundamental pillars — peace, sustainability, and equal opportunity —are facing systematic assaults from political actors seeking to drag the world back into a "dark past." Highlighting Spain's foreign policy actions, Sanchez cited sanctions against Russia and Madrid's arms embargo on the Israeli government, reaffirming an "unequivocal" condemnation of the "genocide that Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza." Sanchez denounced what he characterised as a "planned and coordinated demolition attempt" directed at weakening multilateral institutions: "They start by questioning the rules, then they break them, knowing well that nobody will dare to hold them accountable. They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies like this one. They obstruct these organisations' ability to act, so then write them off as useless entities that we can do without." Despite these challenges, he urged member states to rebuild trust in the UN. Turning to succession, Sanchez insisted the next secretary-general should be a Latin American woman — noting that all nine postholders to date have been men — describing it as a "historic debt that we must settle." Addressing migration in the North African enclave of Ceuta, where roughly 72,000 people crossed irregularly in late July, Sanchez pledged Spain will respect human rights rather than "turn migrants into the enemy."

extraction.body: The General Assembly met on Thursday to examine the Security Council’s latest veto , cast by China and Russia over a United States-backed sanctions panel of experts on Iran nuclear facilities. Many nations have called for removing or limiting veto power in the Council, but reform of the 15-member organ remains a work in progress. At last year’s annual veto debate, then-General Assembly president Annalena Baerbock called repeated veto use a “ poster child ” for global gridlock. Thursday’s debate was triggered by the assembly’s landmark veto initiative, established in 2022. Khalilur Rahman, president of the assembly’s 81st session, said the veto initiative “cannot substitute for effective Security Council action”. Each invocation of the initiative “ highlights both the value of this mechanism and the circumstances that make it necessary ” and affirms the assembly’s complementary role, ensuring that veto use is accompanied by transparency, explanation and consideration by the wider membership. While the initiative does not override the veto, it guarantees a public and accountable debate on each use and its implications in the General Assembly, where there is no veto power. During the debate, Deputy Permanent Representative Sun Lei of China said that his delegation voted against the draft resolution to “uphold a correct sense of right and wrong”. The current impasse on the sanctions panel arises from the United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action on Iran’s nuclear facilities – the Iran nuclear deal of 2015 – its campaign of “maximum pressure” and its “two rounds of strikes against Iran in the midst of negotiations”. Meanwhile, other delegates argued for extending the panel’s mandate. “No UN Member State should prevent the UN Security Council from functioning properly and being fully operational,” said Hedda Samson, Deputy Head of the European Union delegation, noting that the need for a panel of experts is “even great today”. Following Thursday’s debate, the assembly president will send a summary of discussions back to the Security Council. At the outset of the meeting, Mr. Rahman said the assembly and the council “serve humanity best when they operate in balance”, each fulfilling its distinct but complementary responsibilities under the UN Charter . “ Let us, therefore, use this debate not to exacerbate tensions or assign blame, but to clarify positions, identify common ground for constructive solutions and chart a credible path forward to support dialogue and diplomacy and ultimately restore trust in the organization and its ability to deliver,” he said. The United Nations (UN) Assistant Secretary-General for the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific stressed that the situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory is “steadily worsening”, and that rampant settler violence, displacement, and accelerating settlement activity are eroding the prospects for a political process and a resolution to the conflict based on a viable two-State solution. On 27 April, the UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process commended the Palestinian Central Elections Commission for successfully administering the 25 April local elections and ensuring a credible process despite significant constraints, including the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the severe movement and access restrictions in the West Bank. UN human rights experts condemned Israel’s law approved by the Knesset on 30 March, which by effectively providing for the death penalty solely against Palestinians constitutes “a discriminatory regime of capital punishment” and a violation of Israel’s obligations under international human rights law. Similarly, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, condemned the law and expressed indignation at the “sharp deterioration in the human rights of Palestinians in the Occupied Palestinian Territory since the start of the regional hostilities on 28 February”. Further, UN human rights experts called to end Israeli military attacks affecting civilian shelters in Gaza and expressed serious concern over the forced displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, stressing that “the scale and pattern of these actions” showed “the ongoing broader policy of ethnic cleansing across the occupied Palestinian territory”. In a 30 April statement, UN human rights experts expressed concern that “Israeli sexual violence has become embedded in Palestinians’ daily lives under occupation”. “It is intersecting, structural and systematic, and operates as a tool of control, subjugation and dispossession”, they said. They stated dismay at the “inaction of the international community that permits total impunity”. In an advocacy brief released on 17 April, the UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women) reported that deaths of women and girls “reached levels unseen before in previous wars on Gaza”. With a peaking during periods of intensified violence, women and girls continue to be killed despite the October 2025 ceasefire agreement to total of more than 38,000 deaths between October 2023 and December 2025. At the same time, UN Women warned of the deepening health risks for women and girls due to displacement and systematic collapse of reproductive health services, and of the long-term social and protection impact of a rise in women-headed households. The UN Population Fund (UNFPA) sounded the alarm on a surge in child marriage and adolescent pregnancy under the pressure of war. UNFPA analysis showed that child marriage is “increasingly driven by survival, not choice”, as a coping mechanism for families facing extreme poverty and displacement. The World Health Organisation (WHO) confirmed that a person contracted to provide services to it in Gaza was killed on 7 April during a security incident and announced suspension of medical evacuations through Rafah crossing until further notice. The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) expressed outrage at the killing of two truck drivers, whom it had contracted to provide clean water to families in Gaza in an incident on 17 April. The UN Country Team in the Occupied Palestinian Territory and partners condemned the killing and called for the protection of civilians, including humanitarian workers and essential service providers, an obligation under international humanitarian law, to be upheld. On 20 April, the World Bank, the European Union and the UN released the “ Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment ” (RDNA), which estimates recovery and reconstruction needs at around USD 71.4 billion. On 28 April, the UN launched the Horizon Fund , co-chaired by the Palestinian Prime Minister and the UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, to support early recovery and resilience-building efforts, economic revitalization, livelihood recovery, and governance strengthening to promote social cohesion and stability, with a primary focus on Gaza. On 13 April, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that the Israeli authorities reopened Zikim crossing into northern Gaza after its closure for more than 40 days. Collection and offloading activities at this crossing are allowed only on alternating days, however. The Annual Compilation of UN Reports on the Question of Palestine (2025) brings together key UN reports, briefings and technical assessments published in 2025. Prepared by UN entities and its affiliated agencies, it reflects the breadth of work across political, legal, humanitarian, human rights, social, and economic dimensions, highlighting developments in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem. All reports are available on the UNISPAL website. The Annual Compilation of UN Resolutions on the Question of Palestine (2025) presents selected resolutions, decisions and voting records adopted in 2025 by the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council and Human Rights Council. Prepared by DPR, the compilation highlights the ongoing work of the UN system in addressing the question of Palestine. All resolutions are available on the UNISPAL website.

extraction.body: Greece is the president of the Security Council in October. Council members adopted the provisional programme of work for the month earlier today (1 October). Greece has chosen to organise two signature events. The first is a high-level briefing on emerging technologies , with an emphasis on maritime security, under the “Maintenance of international peace and security” agenda item. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis is expected to chair the meeting. The second signature event is a briefing on children and armed conflict to mark the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the children and armed conflict mandate by the General Assembly. Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs Giorgos Gerapetritis is expected to chair the meeting. Briefings are expected from Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict Vanessa Frazier, UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell, African Union (AU) Special Envoy for Children Affected by Armed Conflict Jainaba Jagne, and a civil society representative. The Security Council will hold its annual open debate on women, peace and security (WPS) in October. Gerapetritis is expected to chair the meeting, which will be titled “Women, peace and security in the next quarter-century: fulfilling the promise through implementation”. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, UN Women Executive Director Sima Sami Bahous, and a woman civil society representative are the anticipated briefers. The Security Council is also scheduled to hold its annual private meeting with the president of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Judge Yuji Iwasawa. Tomorrow (2 October), Council members are expected to hold an informal interactive dialogue (IID) on the implementation of resolution 2744 of 19 July 2024, which strengthened the mandate of the Focal Point for Delisting and re-established the Informal Working Group (IWG) of the Security Council on General UN Security Council Sanctions Issues. Yvonne Ching Ling Lee, the Focal Point for Delisting, is expected to brief at the meeting, which is being organised by Greece and Pakistan. This month, the Council will hold its annual briefing on cooperation between the UN and regional and sub-regional organisations , focusing on the AU. Briefings are expected from Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the AU and Head of the UN Office to the AU (UNOAU) Parfait Onanga-Anyanga and AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security Bankole Adeoye. AU Peace and Security Council (AUPSC) members will travel to New York for the 20th annual joint consultative meeting between the Security Council and the AUPSC, to be held on 23 October. (The annual meeting rotates between New York and Addis Ababa, the home of the AU headquarters.) The joint consultative meeting will be preceded by the 11th informal joint seminar of members of the Security Council and the AUPSC on 22 October, which will be held in a retreat format at the Greentree Foundation in Manhasset, New York. Several other African issues are on the programme of work this month. Regarding Sudan , the Security Council is expected to vote on a draft resolution extending the 1591 Sudan sanctions regime. It will also receive the regular 120-day briefing on the situation in the country. A UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA) official and Personal Envoy of the UN Secretary-General for Sudan Pekka Haavisto are expected to brief. The meeting may also feature a briefing on the work of the 1591 Sudan Sanctions Committee. If the allocation of subsidiary body chairs is not decided by the time of the meeting, Greece may brief in its capacity as Council president. Closed consultations are scheduled to follow the open briefing. The Council expects to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) , which expires on 31 October. Ahead of the mandate renewal, the Council will hold a private meeting with MINURSO troop-contributing countries, at which Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Western Sahara and Head of MINURSO Alexander Ivanko will participate. Council members will also receive a briefing in consultations from Ivanko and Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Western Sahara Staffan de Mistura. The Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for the Great Lakes Region , Huang Xia, is expected to provide the biannual briefing to the Council on the implementation of the 2013 Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework (PSC-F) for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the Great Lakes region. Closed consultations are scheduled to follow the open briefing. Council members expect to vote on a draft resolution renewing the mandate of the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) ahead of its 31 October expiry. Prior to that, the Council will hold its bimonthly briefing on the situation in Libya, at which Special Representative and Head of UNSMIL Hanna Serwaa Tetteh is expected to brief. Closed consultations are scheduled to follow the open briefing. There will be a briefing, followed by consultations, on the work of the UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) , which will feature a briefing by Special Representative of the Secretary-General for the Central African Republic (CAR) and Head of MINUSCA Valentine Rugwabiza. The Council will also hold a private meeting with MINUSCA troop-contributing countries, at which Rugwabiza is expected to participate. Several Middle Eastern issues will be addressed in October. The Security Council will hold its quarterly open debate on “The situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question” , which Gerapetritis is expected to chair. The anticipated briefer is Acting Special Coordinator and Resident Coordinator at the Office of the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process (UNSCO) Ramiz Alakbarov. Assistant Secretary-General for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific Mohamed Khaled Khiari will also brief Council members in closed consultations on the work of the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) in the Golan. The Council will also hold its monthly briefing on Yemen . Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg and an official from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) are expected to brief. A civil society representative may also brief. Closed consultations are scheduled to follow the open briefing. There will be a meeting on political and humanitarian developments in Syria . The anticipated briefers are Deputy Special Envoy for Syria Claudio Cordone, an OCHA official, and a civil society representative. On Lebanon , Council members are expected to be briefed in closed consultations by Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo on the Secretary-General’s report on the implementation of resolution 1559 . (Adopted in 2004, the resolution called for the withdrawal of foreign forces from Lebanon, the disarmament of all militias, and the extension of government control over the whole Lebanese territory.) Members are also likely to continue considering options for possible arrangements after the termination of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to support the continued implementation of resolution 1701 , which in 2006 called for a cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. The Security Council is expected to hold a meeting on the Iraq-Kuwait file. The meeting will feature a briefing on the Secretary-General’s report on the implementation of resolution 2792 of 17 September 2025, which authorised the appointment of a Senior Representative with a mandate to promote, support, and facilitate efforts to repatriate or return missing Kuwaiti and third country nationals and missing Kuwaiti property. Senior Representative Mari Yamashita is the anticipated briefer. Two issues in the Americas will be discussed this month. The Council expects to renew the 2653 Haiti sanctions regime ahead of its 17 October expiry. It also plans to hold a briefing, followed by consultations, on the situation in Haiti. Briefings are expected from Special Representative and Head of the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH) Carlos Ruiz Massieu, Special Representative for the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) Jack Christofides, and a civil society representative. The Council expects to vote on a draft resolution renewing the mandate of the UN Verification Mission in Colombia before its 31 October expiry. Ahead of that, it will also hold its quarterly meeting on Colombia. Special Representative and Head of the UN Verification Mission in Colombia Miroslav Jenča is the anticipated briefer. Regarding European issues, the Council will hold its semi-annual briefing on the situation in Kosovo . Special Representative and Head of the UN Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK) Peter Due is expected to brief. The semi-annual debate on Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) will be held in October. The Council is also expected to vote at the end of the month on the reauthorisation of the EU-led multinational stabilisation force in BiH (EUFOR ALTHEA) prior to its 1 November expiry. As in previous months, the Council may hold one or more meetings on Ukraine in October. Council members will continue following closely the crisis in the Middle East and any spillover effects, such as disruption to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Additionally, they are likely to continue monitoring developments in Ethiopia. In October, Council members are expected to continue conducting “straw polls” to gauge support for candidates for the position of UN Secretary-General . During today’s press briefing on this month’s programme of work, Ambassador Aglaia Balta (Greece) said that “October is the month when we need to make progress and even agree on the new Secretary-General”. She added that the presidency intends to continue consulting with other Council members on the matter, including on the use of colour-coded ballots. coreStoryFacts.text: On 28 April, at the quarterly open debate of Security Council on the situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question, the Vice Chair of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People warned about the continuing humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza.

UN human rights experts condemned Israel’s law approved by the Knesset on 30 March, which by effectively providing for the death penalty solely against Palestinians constitutes “a discriminatory regime of capital punishment” and a violation of Israel’s obligations under international human rights law.
“It is intersecting, structural and systematic, and operates as a tool of control, subjugation and dispossession”, they said.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) confirmed that a person contracted to provide services to it in Gaza was killed on 7 April during a security incident and announced suspension of medical evacuations through Rafah crossing until further notice.

The UN Country Team in the Occupied Palestinian Territory and partners condemned the killing and called for the protection of civilians, including humanitarian workers and essential service providers, an obligation under international humanitarian law, to be upheld.

On 20 April, the World Bank, the European Union and the UN released the “ Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment ” (RDNA), which estimates recovery and reconstruction needs at around USD 71.4 billion.

extraction.body: Disclaimer : The texts and links cited in this Monthly Bulletin have been reproduced in their original form . The Division for Palestinian Rights is consequently not responsible for the views, positions or discrepancies contained in these texts. On 28 April, at the quarterly open debate of Security Council on the situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question, the Vice Chair of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People warned about the continuing humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza. He also condemned the continuing settler violence in the West Bank and the Israeli authorities’ measures aimed at changing the demographic, religious, and cultural character of East Jerusalem, and called for the full implementation of the New York Declaration . The United Nations (UN) Assistant Secretary-General for the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific stressed that the situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory is “steadily worsening”, and that rampant settler violence, displacement, and accelerating settlement activity are eroding the prospects for a political process and a resolution to the conflict based on a viable two-State solution. On 27 April, the UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process commended the Palestinian Central Elections Commission for successfully administering the 25 April local elections and ensuring a credible process despite significant constraints, including the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the severe movement and access restrictions in the West Bank. UN human rights experts condemned Israel’s law approved by the Knesset on 30 March, which by effectively providing for the death penalty solely against Palestinians constitutes “a discriminatory regime of capital punishment” and a violation of Israel’s obligations under international human rights law. Similarly, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, condemned the law and expressed indignation at the “sharp deterioration in the human rights of Palestinians in the Occupied Palestinian Territory since the start of the regional hostilities on 28 February”. Further, UN human rights experts called to end Israeli military attacks affecting civilian shelters in Gaza and expressed serious concern over the forced displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, stressing that “the scale and pattern of these actions” showed “the ongoing broader policy of ethnic cleansing across the occupied Palestinian territory”. In a 30 April statement, UN human rights experts expressed concern that “Israeli sexual violence has become embedded in Palestinians’ daily lives under occupation”. “It is intersecting, structural and systematic, and operates as a tool of control, subjugation and dispossession”, they said. They stated dismay at the “inaction of the international community that permits total impunity”. In an advocacy brief released on 17 April, the UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women) reported that deaths of women and girls “reached levels unseen before in previous wars on Gaza”. With a peaking during periods of intensified violence, women and girls continue to be killed despite the October 2025 ceasefire agreement to total of more than 38,000 deaths between October 2023 and December 2025. At the same time, UN Women warned of the deepening health risks for women and girls due to displacement and systematic collapse of reproductive health services, and of the long-term social and protection impact of a rise in women-headed households. The UN Population Fund (UNFPA) sounded the alarm on a surge in child marriage and adolescent pregnancy under the pressure of war. UNFPA analysis showed that child marriage is “increasingly driven by survival, not choice”, as a coping mechanism for families facing extreme poverty and displacement. The World Health Organisation (WHO) confirmed that a person contracted to provide services to it in Gaza was killed on 7 April during a security incident and announced suspension of medical evacuations through Rafah crossing until further notice. The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) expressed outrage at the killing of two truck drivers, whom it had contracted to provide clean water to families in Gaza in an incident on 17 April. The UN Country Team in the Occupied Palestinian Territory and partners condemned the killing and called for the protection of civilians, including humanitarian workers and essential service providers, an obligation under international humanitarian law, to be upheld. On 20 April, the World Bank, the European Union and the UN released the “ Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment ” (RDNA), which estimates recovery and reconstruction needs at around USD 71.4 billion. On 28 April, the UN launched the Horizon Fund , co-chaired by the Palestinian Prime Minister and the UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, to support early recovery and resilience-building efforts, economic revitalization, livelihood recovery, and governance strengthening to promote social cohesion and stability, with a primary focus on Gaza. On 13 April, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that the Israeli authorities reopened Zikim crossing into northern Gaza after its closure for more than 40 days. Collection and offloading activities at this crossing are allowed only on alternating days, however. The Annual Compilation of UN Reports on the Question of Palestine (2025) brings together key UN reports, briefings and technical assessments published in 2025. Prepared by UN entities and its affiliated agencies, it reflects the breadth of work across political, legal, humanitarian, human rights, social, and economic dimensions, highlighting developments in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem. All reports are available on the UNISPAL website. The Annual Compilation of UN Resolutions on the Question of Palestine (2025) presents selected resolutions, decisions and voting records adopted in 2025 by the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council and Human Rights Council. Prepared by DPR, the compilation highlights the ongoing work of the UN system in addressing the question of Palestine. All resolutions are available on the UNISPAL website.

extraction.body: Greece is the president of the Security Council in October. Council members adopted the provisional programme of work for the month earlier today (1 October). Greece has chosen to organise two signature events. The first is a high-level briefing on emerging technologies , with an emphasis on maritime security, under the “Maintenance of international peace and security” agenda item. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis is expected to chair the meeting. The second signature event is a briefing on children and armed conflict to mark the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the children and armed conflict mandate by the General Assembly. Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs Giorgos Gerapetritis is expected to chair the meeting. Briefings are expected from Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict Vanessa Frazier, UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell, African Union (AU) Special Envoy for Children Affected by Armed Conflict Jainaba Jagne, and a civil society representative. The Security Council will hold its annual open debate on women, peace and security (WPS) in October. Gerapetritis is expected to chair the meeting, which will be titled “Women, peace and security in the next quarter-century: fulfilling the promise through implementation”. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, UN Women Executive Director Sima Sami Bahous, and a woman civil society representative are the anticipated briefers. The Security Council is also scheduled to hold its annual private meeting with the president of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Judge Yuji Iwasawa. Tomorrow (2 October), Council members are expected to hold an informal interactive dialogue (IID) on the implementation of resolution 2744 of 19 July 2024, which strengthened the mandate of the Focal Point for Delisting and re-established the Informal Working Group (IWG) of the Security Council on General UN Security Council Sanctions Issues. Yvonne Ching Ling Lee, the Focal Point for Delisting, is expected to brief at the meeting, which is being organised by Greece and Pakistan. This month, the Council will hold its annual briefing on cooperation between the UN and regional and sub-regional organisations , focusing on the AU. Briefings are expected from Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the AU and Head of the UN Office to the AU (UNOAU) Parfait Onanga-Anyanga and AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security Bankole Adeoye. AU Peace and Security Council (AUPSC) members will travel to New York for the 20th annual joint consultative meeting between the Security Council and the AUPSC, to be held on 23 October. (The annual meeting rotates between New York and Addis Ababa, the home of the AU headquarters.) The joint consultative meeting will be preceded by the 11th informal joint seminar of members of the Security Council and the AUPSC on 22 October, which will be held in a retreat format at the Greentree Foundation in Manhasset, New York. Several other African issues are on the programme of work this month. Regarding Sudan , the Security Council is expected to vote on a draft resolution extending the 1591 Sudan sanctions regime. It will also receive the regular 120-day briefing on the situation in the country. A UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA) official and Personal Envoy of the UN Secretary-General for Sudan Pekka Haavisto are expected to brief. The meeting may also feature a briefing on the work of the 1591 Sudan Sanctions Committee. If the allocation of subsidiary body chairs is not decided by the time of the meeting, Greece may brief in its capacity as Council president. Closed consultations are scheduled to follow the open briefing. passages: The proposal "would provide a clear regulatory framework for the custody of crypto assets, giving investment advisers and funds a compliant pathway where none existed before — and replacing the grey of uncertainty created by custody rules crafted for a bygone era,” said SEC Chairman Paul Atkins in a statement.

Atkins said that existing custody rules "were designed to protect the assets of advisory clients and regulated funds from loss, theft, misuse, and misappropriation," but they only consider "the custody and safekeeping only of traditional assets — an untenable situation in the 21st century."
The latest move to advance a pro-crypto U.S. securities agenda comes the day before the exit of Commissioner Hester Peirce, who has led the agency's Crypto Task Force since its inception.
With the movement on the custody issue, the SEC has now put a checkmark in every major topic on the crypto agenda originally set out by Atkins.

extraction.body: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is aiming to clarify how investment firms can handle and keep customer crypto assets in a new rule proposed Thursday. The proposal "would provide a clear regulatory framework for the custody of crypto assets, giving investment advisers and funds a compliant pathway where none existed before — and replacing the grey of uncertainty created by custody rules crafted for a bygone era,” said SEC Chairman Paul Atkins in a statement. The SEC’s new approach would clarify what kinds of companies can properly hold crypto assets and how investment advisers and regulated funds need to keep records and make federal disclosures. It also offers new clarifications of industry practices and auditing requirements. Atkins said that existing custody rules "were designed to protect the assets of advisory clients and regulated funds from loss, theft, misuse, and misappropriation," but they only consider "the custody and safekeeping only of traditional assets — an untenable situation in the 21st century." The newly proposed rule, open for a 60-day public comment period, would also allow for self-custody of crypto assets "under certain circumstances" and permit the use of state-chartered trusts as custodians. The latest move to advance a pro-crypto U.S. securities agenda comes the day before the exit of Commissioner Hester Peirce, who has led the agency's Crypto Task Force since its inception. She leaves on Friday and will be a professor in Virginia, leaving the agency with just two . With the movement on the custody issue, the SEC has now put a checkmark in every major topic on the crypto agenda originally set out by Atkins. According to the 760-page proposal , the SEC will allow for self-custody by advisers seeking to hold their clients' funds. The agency is using the term "self-custody" as an asset management firm practice, not how crypto companies typically use the term. It would first require that an adviser can’t find a qualified custodian ready to take the assets, which would likely be an unusual circumstance after the rule is implemented, and it also requires certain expertise for the investment firm to hold crypto assets. passages: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is aiming to clarify how investment firms can handle and keep customer crypto assets in a new rule proposed Thursday .

The proposal "would provide a clear regulatory framework for the custody of crypto assets, giving investment advisers and funds a compliant pathway where none existed before — and replacing the grey of uncertainty created by custody rules crafted for a bygone era,” said SEC Chairman Paul Atkins in a statement .

The SEC’s new approach would clarify what kinds of companies can properly hold crypto assets and how investment advisers and regulated funds need to keep records and make federal disclosures. It would also offer new clarifications of industry practices and auditing requirements.

According to the 760-page proposal , the SEC will allow for self-custody by advisers seeking to hold their clients' funds. The agency is using the term "self-custody" as an asset management firm practice, not how crypto companies typically use the term. It would first require that an adviser can’t find a qualified custodian ready to take the assets, which would likely be an unusual circumstance after the rule is implemented, and it also requires certain expertise for the investment firm to hold crypto assets. Additionally, that ability to hold their own clients assets would have to be reviewed every quarter to see if a custodian has become available, an SEC official said.

The official granted that the circumstance for self-custody — which stems from an industry request to the Crypto Task Force — would likely be unusual, though it could apply to a newly launched token that custodians didn't yet support.

Atkins said that existing custody rules "were designed to protect the assets of advisory clients and regulated funds from loss, theft, misuse, and misappropriation," but they only consider "the custody and safekeeping only of traditional assets — an untenable situation in the 21st century."
The newly proposed rule, open for a 60-day public comment period, would also permit the use of state-chartered trusts as custodians.

extraction.body: The University of Hawaiʻi and the University of Massachusetts have agreed to collaborate on research and education focused on strengthening energy systems, critical infrastructure and national security, with presidents from both systems putting pen to paper Thursday at Bachman Hall on the UH Mānoa campus. UH President Wendy F. Hensel and UMass President Marty Meehan signed the five-year memorandum of understanding, according to University of Hawaiʻi System News . The agreement sets up a framework for the two university systems to pursue joint research, student and faculty exchanges, training programs and other initiatives, rather than locking in any specific projects right away. Potential collaboration areas span cyber-physical systems, microgrids, advanced manufacturing, autonomous systems, maritime technologies and sensing, per the same announcement. The agreement also calls for exploring research and workforce development opportunities aligned with U.S. Department of Defense priorities, with an initial focus on energy resilience and critical-infrastructure protection. The partnership recognizes the shared importance of resilient infrastructure in Hawaiʻi and Massachusetts — two states, the university system noted, with extensive coastal and maritime environments. Hensel said Hawaiʻi has a responsibility to use its expertise and unique position in the islands to address challenges both locally and across the nation, adding that Hawaiʻi is an important place to develop and test solutions that can strengthen resilience. Meehan said the agreement creates opportunities for researchers, faculty and students from both institutions to work together on challenges affecting communities across the country, and that the two university systems share a commitment to research and education addressing real-world problems. He also said the partnership can help prepare students for the workforce of the future. UH Regent Neil Abercrombie, who attended the signing, said the partnership was a perfect opportunity for the two universities. Abercrombie and Meehan reportedly first crossed paths years earlier while both were serving in the U.S. House of Representatives. Also on hand for the signing were UH Mānoa Chancellor Vassilis Syrmos, UH Board of Regents Chair Lauren Akitake, UH Director of Federal Relations Anthony Ching and UMass Lowell Associate Vice Chancellor for Sustainability and Enterprise Development Ruairi O’Mahony. Microgrids, one of the technologies flagged for potential joint research, are systems that can disconnect from the main power grid and operate independently in what's known as island mode, according to MassCEC . That ability lets a facility keep its lights on even when the broader grid goes down — exactly the kind of resilience both states have been chasing independently for years. In Massachusetts, MassCEC-backed upgrades gave UMass Amherst more than $1.6 million in federal funds to overhaul its campus microgrid, including new automatic transfer switches at five buildings, protective relay upgrades at 45 locations and an underground duct bank, the organization notes. That campus system now includes advanced battery storage alongside the largest behind-the-meter solar array in the state. MassCEC also funded a separate microgrid for the Wakefield Municipal Gas and Light Department, which received over $2.8 million to support its Energy Park project serving Wakefield High School and Northeast Metropolitan Regional Vocational High School. Hawaiʻi has its own microgrid efforts already underway. Hensel Phelps, Sustainability Partners and the Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation broke ground on two microgrid projects on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi featuring solar canopies, battery storage and EV charging stations, according to Solar Builder Magazine . The Oʻahu system is set to serve HDOT Highways' Oʻahu District Main Office Facility near downtown Honolulu. The new UH-UMass pact's nod toward Department of Defense-aligned research echoes work already happening at UMass Lowell. The U.S. Navy's Office of Naval Research awarded UMass Lowell and Stony Brook University a grant to advance energy-resilience technologies, with UMass Lowell putting the figure at $6.3 million, while Stony Brook University has separately described an earlier Navy grant for similar energy-resiliency research as totaling $7.36 million and running through fall 2022. Researchers on the UMass Lowell-Stony Brook effort are working across 12 projects in four focus areas: power-grid management, structural health monitoring of energy infrastructure, energy storage and materials, and fuels and power systems. Crucially, UH News notes the new memorandum is a framework rather than a commitment to specific projects — individual research initiatives between UH and UMass would still need to be developed through separate agreements. Whether any of the listed collaboration areas, from microgrids to autonomous systems, actually advance beyond this starting point will depend on those future deals. extraction.body: The University of Hawaiʻi and the University of Massachusetts have agreed to collaborate on research and education focused on strengthening energy systems, critical infrastructure and national security, with presidents from both systems putting pen to paper Thursday at Bachman Hall on the UH Mānoa campus. UH President Wendy F. Hensel and UMass President Marty Meehan signed the five-year memorandum of understanding, according to University of Hawaiʻi System News . The agreement sets up a framework for the two university systems to pursue joint research, student and faculty exchanges, training programs and other initiatives, rather than locking in any specific projects right away. Potential collaboration areas span cyber-physical systems, microgrids, advanced manufacturing, autonomous systems, maritime technologies and sensing, per the same announcement. The agreement also calls for exploring research and workforce development opportunities aligned with U.S. Department of Defense priorities, with an initial focus on energy resilience and critical-infrastructure protection. The partnership recognizes the shared importance of resilient infrastructure in Hawaiʻi and Massachusetts — two states, the university system noted, with extensive coastal and maritime environments. Hensel said Hawaiʻi has a responsibility to use its expertise and unique position in the islands to address challenges both locally and across the nation, adding that Hawaiʻi is an important place to develop and test solutions that can strengthen resilience. Meehan said the agreement creates opportunities for researchers, faculty and students from both institutions to work together on challenges affecting communities across the country, and that the two university systems share a commitment to research and education addressing real-world problems. He also said the partnership can help prepare students for the workforce of the future. UH Regent Neil Abercrombie, who attended the signing, said the partnership was a perfect opportunity for the two universities. Abercrombie and Meehan reportedly first crossed paths years earlier while both were serving in the U.S. House of Representatives. Also on hand for the signing were UH Mānoa Chancellor Vassilis Syrmos, UH Board of Regents Chair Lauren Akitake, UH Director of Federal Relations Anthony Ching and UMass Lowell Associate Vice Chancellor for Sustainability and Enterprise Development Ruairi O’Mahony. Microgrids, one of the technologies flagged for potential joint research, are systems that can disconnect from the main power grid and operate independently in what's known as island mode, according to MassCEC . That ability lets a facility keep its lights on even when the broader grid goes down — exactly the kind of resilience both states have been chasing independently for years. In Massachusetts, MassCEC-backed upgrades gave UMass Amherst more than $1.6 million in federal funds to overhaul its campus microgrid, including new automatic transfer switches at five buildings, protective relay upgrades at 45 locations and an underground duct bank, the organization notes. That campus system now includes advanced battery storage alongside the largest behind-the-meter solar array in the state. MassCEC also funded a separate microgrid for the Wakefield Municipal Gas and Light Department, which received over $2.8 million to support its Energy Park project serving Wakefield High School and Northeast Metropolitan Regional Vocational High School. Hawaiʻi has its own microgrid efforts already underway. Hensel Phelps, Sustainability Partners and the Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation broke ground on two microgrid projects on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi featuring solar canopies, battery storage and EV charging stations, according to Solar Builder Magazine . The Oʻahu system is set to serve HDOT Highways' Oʻahu District Main Office Facility near downtown Honolulu. The new UH-UMass pact's nod toward Department of Defense-aligned research echoes work already happening at UMass Lowell. The U.S. Navy's Office of Naval Research awarded UMass Lowell and Stony Brook University a grant to advance energy-resilience technologies, with UMass Lowell putting the figure at $6.3 million, while Stony Brook University has separately described an earlier Navy grant for similar energy-resiliency research as totaling $7.36 million and running through fall 2022. Researchers on the UMass Lowell-Stony Brook effort are working across 12 projects in four focus areas: power-grid management, structural health monitoring of energy infrastructure, energy storage and materials, and fuels and power systems. Crucially, UH News notes the new memorandum is a framework rather than a commitment to specific projects — individual research initiatives between UH and UMass would still need to be developed through separate agreements. Whether any of the listed collaboration areas, from microgrids to autonomous systems, actually advance beyond this starting point will depend on those future deals. Apple retail stores received confidential boxes earlier this week featuring "Do Not Open Until October 8" stickers on them. They are believed to contain new visual merchandise, which enables workers to update labels, graphics, and product layouts in stores around the release of new products. MacRumors received a tip-off about the boxes earlier this week, which it has now independently verified. There is a possibility that the materials relate to the iPhone Duo , but it seems more likely given their confidentiality and timing that they relate to the rumored launch of Apple's smart home hub , alongside a new Apple TV 4K, and the HomePod mini 2. Yesterday, Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said that Apple plans to introduce these three long-awaited new devices on Tuesday, October 13 . If Apple announces the new devices sometime in the week of Monday, October 5, Apple Stores would need to update their displays for launch on October 13. For now, the exact timing of the announcement of the trio is unclear. Gurman's report used indeterminate wording, simply saying that Apple would "push into the smart-home market on October 13." sources.title: Kevin Mandia’s new ‘agent swarm’ security startup Armadin raises $255.5M at $2.5B valuation
passages: Kevin Mandia, best known as the founder of cybersecurity startup Mandiant, which sold to Google for $5.4 billion in 2022 , has raised $255.5 million for his latest startup, Armadin, at a valuation of more than $2.5 billion, the company announced on Thursday.
Armadin is offering enterprises a new kind of always-on security by reimagining defense testing for the AI era.

Instead of traditional penetration tests, where hired guns attempt to break in and report on the weaknesses they find, Armadin runs always-on agentic swarms, who chain together vulnerabilities to hack in.
The idea is to help organizations find and seal holes before any bad guys (or even AI labs with rogue agents ) can use agentic tech against them.
The new round comes just six months after Armadin raised a $190 million Series A in March.

sources.title: The founder’s guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know
passages: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era?
Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground.
If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone.
The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.
This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it.
Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.
That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point.
And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists.
Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup.
For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.
Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here .
Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app.
You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.
Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.
The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds.
You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations.
It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.
Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand.
And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times.

If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, with a special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year .
But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

extraction.body: With Crew-13, Jessica Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space. A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station. Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT (15:10 UTC) Thursday. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening. The launch was delayed from mid-September to replace a balky valve in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system, a task that involved cutting into a propellant line inside the ship to swap out a faulty component. Jessica Watkins, a 38-year-old geologist turned astronaut, leads the four-person crew sent into orbit Thursday, becoming the first Black woman to command a spacecraft. Watkins is the only veteran astronaut on the mission —designated Crew-13 —after spending 170 days in orbit on a long-duration spaceflight in 2022. Pilot Luke Delaney, a Marine Corps veteran, was seated next to Watkins for the Dragon spacecraft’s ascent into orbit. Two international crew members rounded out the Crew-13 team: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, a former pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, and Sergey Teteryatnikov, a Russian cosmonaut who served as a naval engineer before his selection to the Roscosmos Cosmonaut Corps in 2021. Kutryk and his wife Heather are expecting their third child later this year. It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter , Abigail Mae, in Houston. “Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done. But that has always been the nature of exploration,” Kutryk wrote on X . Watkins and her crewmates were on course to reach the International Space Station (ISS) about eight hours after launch, the fastest-ever launch-to-docking transit to the ISS by a US spacecraft. “What an epic ride. What an epic ride it was,” Delaney radioed mission control soon after reaching orbit. “Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for the future of space exploration.” The ISS has been permanently staffed since 2000, with crews flying to and from the orbiting outpost on NASA’s Space Shuttles, Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and most recently, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon. NASA and its international partners plan to keep the space station operating through at least 2030. SpaceX’s plans to retire the Crew Dragon vehicle around 2030 have prompted NASA to work more closely with Boeing to bring its troubled Starliner crew capsule into service. Thursday’s flight was the 13th crew rotation mission launched by SpaceX under a multibillion-dollar contract with NASA, and SpaceX’s 21st human spaceflight overall, including test flights and fully commercial missions. The company’s success with the Crew Dragon spacecraft restored the country’s ability to launch astronauts into orbit after a nine-year gap following the Space Shuttle retirement in 2011, ending NASA’s sole reliance on Russia for crew transportation. NASA’s other commercial crew provider, Boeing, has repeatedly stumbled on a series of test flights with its Starliner spacecraft. SpaceX’s plans to retire Crew Dragon and the Falcon 9 rocket mean the fleets are now well beyond halfway through their operational life. SpaceX has nine more Crew Dragon flights in its backlog, including three additional crew missions to the ISS that NASA recently secured in a $946 million contract extension, bringing NASA’s total contract for 17 SpaceX crew missions to $5.92 billion. That figure is a drop in the bucket next to SpaceX’s projected revenues from its ever-growing Starlink broadband service, the Starship/Super Heavy rocket, and orbital data centers. SpaceX, now a publicly traded company, is prioritizing its most lucrative lines of business, and flights to the ISS aren’t among them. Bill Gerstenmaier, SpaceX’s vice president of build and flight reliability, declined to say in a prelaunch press conference Wednesday if there is a “hard cutoff” for when the company will no longer offer Crew Dragon flights to NASA. The recent contract extension may be the last. “We were just awarded Crew flights 15, 16, and 17, so I think our real focus is to make sure we get the most out of those flights,” Gerstenmaier said. “So we’re working really super hard to make sure that our vehicles are ready, things are ready to go fly, and we’ll keep moving forward.” Notably, SpaceX is winding down Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 at the top of their game. Gerstenmaier pointed to the valve replacement inside the Crew Dragon spacecraft for the Crew-13 mission as evidence of SpaceX’s commitment to fulfilling its contract with NASA. NASA announced a postponement for the Crew-13 launch in late August to give ground teams time to resolve an oxidizer leak inside Dragon’s propulsion system detected during launch preparations at Cape Canaveral. SpaceX traced the leak to a valve. The spacecraft was already loaded with nitrogen tetroxide, or NTO, the volatile, toxic oxidizer used by Dragon’s control thrusters in combination with hydrazine fuel. Teams devised an unprecedented bit of spaceship surgery to replace the valve without draining the propellant and disassembling the spacecraft, steps that would have triggered a much longer delay. The fix involved cutting into the propellant line, removing and replacing the valve, then welding the line together again. It was the first time SpaceX has performed such a repair with a fully assembled Dragon spacecraft loaded with propellant. “By cutting it out, we physically went in and actually cut the valve out of the line,” Gerstenmaier said. “It was welded in place, and then we actually re-welded a new valve in place.” Engineers are testing the bad valve to diagnose the cause of the leak, but NASA officials were pleased with the fix. No leaks were detected during final preparations for launch Thursday, and Dragon’s propulsion system appeared to be functioning well after arriving in orbit. “We looked at the plans, all of the data coming out of that, the welds, the leak, everything looks great,” said Dana Weigel, NASA’s program manager for the International Space Station. [We’re] really happy with how that repair was done.” SpaceX’s preference to cut out the valve in place, rather than take a longer stand-down, kept the Crew-13 mission on track to arrive at the space station in time to replace Crew-12, which will return to Earth in mid-October after eight months in orbit. The Crew Dragon spacecraft was inside SpaceX’s fueling and hazardous processing facility, known as Area 59, at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, not at the company’s usual maintenance hangar a few miles away. “I actually went down and looked at the vehicle itself, got in the clean room, and took a look to see where they actually had to cut the valve out,” Gerstenmaier said. “There was not a lot of room, but there was good access up on the platform. I think the unique aspect of this was the location where it was being done. “We also did it with oxidizer onboard the vehicle, and the oxidizer tank was full, so we made sure that was all clear,” Gerstenmaier said. “We had to get special permission from the [Space Force’s Eastern] Range to do these activities, to do ‘hot work’ with NTO, with nitrogen tetroxide on the vehicle.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

In the Opus 5.5 release , Anthropic boasted that the model “communicates more naturally than prior models,” saying early users “found its writing clearer and easier to follow.”

But while individual tells change, Graphite says the overall number is mostly holding steady. “It’s not like the tells are decreasing,” Druck told TechCrunch. “They are managing to remove the most well-known tells, but other ones pop up. And every model version has its own.”

It’s surprising that tells are so persistent, given the labs’ focus on human-like writing styles. In the Opus 5.5 release , Anthropic boasted that the model “communicates more naturally than prior models,” saying early users “found its writing clearer and easier to follow.”
OpenAI made similar claims when releasing the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna , saying users could “expect to see more clarity, less jargon, [and] fewer odd turns of phrase.”
But Druck is skeptical about how much the labs can do to completely eliminate telltale construction or phrases.

“A general hypothesis I have is that the labs are less able to control some of these things than you might expect,” Druck says. “These are giant models with billions of parameters. They have some finite number of tests they can run, and things slip through.”

sources.title: Musk’s AI chatbot Grok reportedly encouraged Trump to capture  Venezuela’s president
passages: During this meeting, Trump “spent hours” talking to Musk’s Grok chatbot, including asking how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of their president, a source told Time.
Just a few months earlier, in September, Trump began ordering U.S. military strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump alleged were involved in drug trafficking.

While Grok isn’t the only AI model serving the DoD (OpenAI also has an agreement and Anthropic has been in a back-and-forth over how its models can be used for military intelligence and in modern warfare ), Grok may become an even bigger favorite under this administration.
In December 2025, about a month before the U.S. invaded Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, President Trump had a secret meeting with Elon Musk, Time magazine reports.
This was roughly seven months after Musk left his role in the Trump administration at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
People had apparently been turning to Grok asking about the boat strikes and political climate in Venezuela, as The Atlantic reported at the time.
So Grok told Trump that Maduro was a “deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall,” Time reported.

passages: AI agents hacked the hackers - the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) - via two zero-day bugs in its Zammad support platform, abusing the flaws to hijack sessions, run code remotely as the local zammad user, and escalate privileges to root.

The chained exploits took just seconds to move from session hijacking to root access, and on Thursday, the nonprofit bug hunting organization said the miscreants stole data belonging to its volunteer security researchers, including DIVD email addresses and potentially other contact details.
In a subsequent interview with The Register , Garrity said he applauded DIVD’s “brutal honesty” about the breach.
“They're eating their own dog food, which is great, and getting information out quickly to other organizations that potentially use this product so they can take action before they get hit.”®
While the investigation remains ongoing, security researchers applauded DIVD for its transparency in disclosing and responding to the hack.

extraction.body: Chained Zammad flaws enabled session hijacking, code execution, and root escalation in seconds AI agents hacked the hackers - the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) - via two zero-day bugs in its Zammad support platform, abusing the flaws to hijack sessions, run code remotely as the local zammad user, and escalate privileges to root. The chained exploits took just seconds to move from session hijacking to root access, and on Thursday, the nonprofit bug hunting organization said the miscreants stole data belonging to its volunteer security researchers, including DIVD email addresses and potentially other contact details. “We’re still investigating exactly which data of which volunteers is affected,” DIVD said in its incident report . “For DIVD volunteers (and others) this means a higher risk of social engineering, because this makes it easier for someone to pose as a DIVD’er.” A subsequent LinkedIn post advised anyone receiving an email or contact request from someone at DIVD “that feels slightly off” to verify that it’s legit by emailing communications@divd.nl. DIVD is also a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), and it assigned CVE IDs to the now-public security holes in Zammad, an open-source helpdesk and customer support ticketing system. They are CVE-2026-102489 and CVE-2026-102490 , and both bugs received CVSS 4.0 scores of 9.4, when assessed in the chained attack scenario. CVE-2026-102489 enables unauthenticated attackers to achieve remote code execution and leak user sessions, while CVE-2026-102490 allows a local user to elevate their privileges to root. Zammad versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 are vulnerable to CVE-2026-102489, and it also exists in versions 7.0.0 through 7.1.3 - but it’s not exploitable “due to environment conditions,” according to DIVD’s advisory. All Zammad versions are vulnerable to CVE-2026-102490. DIVD advises “all users of Zammad to upgrade to version 7 of Zammad or to take it offline.” According to the nonprofit’s timeline , the attack happened on September 21, when "malicious actors” broke into its IT system via the two zero-days in its ticketing support software. Based on the amount of payload launched by the Falcon 9, they think a similar cost-reduction trajectory will require Starship to fly 370,000 tons of payload into orbit.
That’s something that would take it about 1,800 launches over the next 10 years, or 180 a year — and that’s if it can fly 200 metric tons on each mission.
SpaceX predicts the company will be flying far more than that — Elon Musk has suggested Starship could achieve an hourly flight rate in 2029, for example, but Musk says a lot of things.
Although the researchers stress their analysis isn’t an economic feasibility study, it offers an interesting picture of how the company sees rockets becoming cheaper over time.
Like all data center companies, Google is looking to SpaceX to get its spacecraft off the ground. (Google is also a major investor in SpaceX.)
What sets the Google initiative apart from those startups (and indeed from SpaceX itself) is that it’s a long-term project.
The company had to redo tests blasting the chips in a particle accelerator after they realized the configuration of the chips provided more shielding than they would actually experience.
This produced slightly more errors in the chip’s logic circuitry, but the company is still confident its chips can handle large inference workloads in orbit for the five-year lifespan of a satellite.

“The bandwidth and the latency between TPUs really, really matters when you’re trying to run a multi-rack workload…we’re trying to look ahead to not just what workloads exist today, but where they will be in five years,” Beals said.
Built by Planet Labs , the satellite will prove that a Google Tensor Processing Unit, its competitor to Nvidia’s GPUs, can function in space.
That means supplying a kilowatt of continuous power, cooling the chip, and running a series of models through their paces to see if anything goes wrong.

extraction.body: Google’s prototype of its orbital compute satellite took off today onboard a SpaceX rocket launched from California — the first time the tech giant has sent one of its advanced chips into space. Built by Planet Labs , the satellite will prove that a Google Tensor Processing Unit, its competitor to Nvidia’s GPUs, can function in space. That means supplying a kilowatt of continuous power, cooling the chip, and running a series of models through their paces to see if anything goes wrong. “We’ve done testing on the ground, but you know, there’s no test that’s completely as good as the real thing,” said Travis Beals, the Google executive managing Project Suncatcher , the tech giant’s plan to develop large-scale compute clusters in orbit around the Earth. Once commissioned, the satellite will fire up its TPU in 15-minute bursts to avoid straining the satellite’s power and thermal management systems. This satellite is based on a standard platform built by Planet Labs, but the two companies are working on a demo expected to take flight next year that will see two satellites more purpose-built for advanced compute that can run more substantial workloads. Those future versions will attempt to collaborate via a laser communications link. Suncatcher isn’t the only space AI payload on this SpaceX rocket, which is launching more than 100 different payloads, including missions from Satlyt and Cowboy Space Company. What sets the Google initiative apart from those startups (and indeed from SpaceX itself) is that it’s a long-term project. The focus of this “long-term moonshot,” as Beals puts it, is on building for the space infrastructure and AI workloads that will exist in the future. That’s a big ask for a vehicle that has never flown more than five times in a year. SpaceX predicts the company will be flying far more than that — Elon Musk has suggested Starship could achieve an hourly flight rate in 2029, for example, but Musk says a lot of things.

The good news, at least, in Google’s updated research, is that it seems likely that its chips will survive the radiation of space. The company had to redo tests blasting the chips in a particle accelerator after they realized the configuration of the chips provided more shielding than they would actually experience. This produced slightly more errors in the chip’s logic circuitry, but the company is still confident its chips can handle large inference workloads in orbit for the five-year lifespan of a satellite.

“The error rate is very low if you’re thinking about typical inference operations, right? Like one in a million,” Beals said. “On the other hand, it was already problematic for doing, say, some mega-scale training run where you’re going to have many thousands of chips running for months.”

passages: The major averages posted modest gains in the third quarter, which ended Wednesday, but there were much bigger moves beneath the surface as market leadership shifted.
Software stocks roared back from their artificial intelligence-driven sell off, while chip names cooled after a massive first-half run.
The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) rose 17% during the quarter, compared with an 11% decline for the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX).
Questions for Cramer? Call Cramer: 1-800-743-CNBC

The company unveiled Claudeforce , which includes a plugin that lets customers use Anthropic's Claude to access data stored in Salesforce and perform tasks such as drafting emails and updating records.
Salesforce also delivered a strong quarter and took advantage of its lower share price to buy back stock.
Meanwhile, some previous data center winners cooled off.
Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of CRM, MSFT, and CRWD.
Heading into the new quarter, however, Cramer's biggest concern is whether the Federal Reserve will continue raising interest rates.
The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September, putting pressure on rate-sensitive stocks such as Home Depot .
"Microsoft's rally is just beginning," Cramer said, pointing to strong demand for Copilot, accelerating growth at Azure and signs that its data center investments are beginning to generate returns.

"My big fear right now is the impact of higher interest rates on the stock market," Cramer said, adding that the upcoming earnings season should provide a clearer picture of how higher borrowing costs are affecting companies.
